stem: You are performing a transvaginal ultrasound scan on a 32-year-old woman who is being investigated for abnormal bleeding. The endometrium is diffusely thickened, measuring around 18mm thick.
prompt: What is the LEAST likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Please note that the question asks for the LEAST likely answer.

Endometrial thickening

The normal endometrium is thickest in the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle (days 14-28) and at this stage can measure upto 15mm. In the non-acute setting it is best to time the ultrasound to take place during days 5-10 of the cycle since at this time the endometrium is thinner and there is less variability in thickness between patients. It is therefore easier to conclude on normality or abnormality.

| Differential diagnosis for endometrial thickening (>7mm on day 5-10) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-gestational | Gestational |  |
| Hyperplastic | Endometrial hyperplasia (uniform) | Early pregnancy <5 weeks |
|  | Endometrial polyp (focal) | Ectopic pregnancy |
| Drugs | Hormone replacement therapy | Molar pregnancy |
|  | Tamoxifen (highly variable) | Retained products of conception |
| Neoplastic | Endometrial carcinoma |  |
|  | Some ovarian carcinomas |  |
| Infective/ sequela | Endometritis |  |
|  | Adhesions |  |

There are limits for the thickness of the endometrium at other parts of the cycle which are approximately as follows:

| Endometrial thickness, normal limits |  |
| --- | --- |
| Day 0-7 | <4mm |
| Day 7-14 | <7mm |
| Ovulation | <11mm |
| Day 14-28 | <15mm |
| Post-menopausal | <5mm |

Some literature suggests different limits for referral (for endometrial tissue sampling) of a post-menopausal patient depending on whether there is any bleeding or not however since all patients with post-menopausal bleeding should undergo endometrial sampling anyway, the implications of the endometrial thickness are irrelevant.

Some ovarian tumours cause oestrogenic effects and these can lead to thickening of the endometrium. These are:

Endometroid carcinoma

Clear cell carcinoma

Granulosa cell tumours

Thecomas

Fibrothecomas

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)

PCOS affects around 5% of women and patients experience a broad spectrum of issues with it ranging from being completely asymptomatic through to infertility and other important gynaecological problems.

The typical patient with PCOS is overweight with impaired glucose tolerance. High blood pressure and high lipid levels may be found on blood tests and excess circulating androgen levels cause an increase in the LH to FSH ratio as well as explaining the other physical complaints of many patients such as acne and hirsutism. It should be noted that a diagnosis of PCOS should not be made on the basis of imaging findings.

Patients with PCOS often (but not always) show ovarian enlargement, each with a volume in excess of 15cm3.  There are ususally multiple small cysts within the ovaries; those which give the syndrome its name. These are the developing follicles caused by aberrations in hormone levels. They usually appear around the edge of the ovary, in a subcapsular location, as anechoic rounded cystic structures and there are typically around 5-10 per ovary at any one time but can be many more in number than this. The appearance is sometimes described as looking like a string of pearls. It should be noted however that this appearance can also be seen in otherwise normal women too.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Schomynv CC0

Endometrial hyperplasia occurs due to high oestrogen levels and patients are at increased risk of endometrial carcinoma. When it does occur, endometrial carcinoma may arise at a younger age than the normal population (<40 years)

stem: A 32-year-old man presents for an ultrasound scan with a left testicular lump. The request notes his aFP is raised. The ultrasound scan demonstrates a hypoechoic mass with heterogenous areas and cyst formation. Subsequent imaging demonstrates liver metastases.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Lymphoma

Testicular lymphoma is classically seen in an older man with bilateral hypoechoic lesions.

Teratomas, Yolk sac tumours, Embryonal cell tumours and Choriocarcinomas all fall into the category of Non-seminomatous Germ Cell tumours. Of these, Embryonal cell tumours make up the vast majority.

Teratoma

This is the second most common tumour in boys under 5. aFP is usually normal. Under ultrasound it appears as a heterogenous complex mass.

Yolk sac tumour

This makes up 80% of childhood testicular tumours.This can often present as testicular enlargement without a focal mass. It metastases to lung which is the most common site of recurrent disease.

Embryonal cell tumour

This is the second most common testicular tumour. It is the most aggressive of all testicular tumours with visceral metastases common and 5 year survival of 30%.

Choriocarcinoma

This is a rare tumour affecting 20-30-year-olds with rapid metastases to lung, liver, GI tract, brain. Often causes haemorrhage in both primary and metastatic lesions. Causes gynaecomastia in 10% due to raised serum hCG.

In reality, tumours are often mixed histological types (around 35% cases). Testicular tumours can also be diagnosed with a strong pre-test probability based solely on age as detailed in the table below. In reality, the role of the radiologist however does not need to be as complex as suggesting the final histological diagnosis. Establishing the presence of a testicular mass is sufficient. Patients should then be referred on to the urology MDT. On ultrasound there will be an intratesticular low reflectivity well-defined mass. Colour doppler flow can be seen within the mass.

| Age at diagnosis | Tumour |
| --- | --- |
| 10s | Yolk sac tumour or teratoma |
| 20s and 30s | Choriocarcinoma |
| 30s | Embryonal cell carcinoma |
| 40s | Seminoma |

stem: You are performing an intravenous urogram on a 65-year-old man which shows medial deviation of both ureters around the level of L4/5. You note from the clinical information provided that the gentleman has had long-standing problems with lower back pain in addition to more recent urinary symptoms.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Retroperitoneal fibrosis

Around two thirds of cases are primary autoimmune manifestations as part of the spectrum of IgG4 related disease and these patients respond very well to steroid therapy. The remaining third can arise as a desmoplastic response in patients secondary to a variety of things.

| Causes of retroperitoneal fibrosis |
| --- |
| Connective tissue diseases |
| Aortic aneurysm |
| Nodal metastases (retroperitoneal) |
| Drugs (methylsergide, beta blockers) |
| Lymphoma, Hodgkin disease |
| Radiation therapy |
| MethylsergideUsed in prophylactic treatment of migraines and cluster headaches |

Clinically patients present insidiously with back pain, weight loss and malaise. Renal failure and hypertension also occur due to compression of the renal arteries.

On CT there will be a periaortic mass. In the acute inflammatory phase contrast enhancement may be seen. One of the main differential diagnoses is Lymphoma. Retroperitoneal fibrosis causes a 'tapering down' appearance to the aorta, as opposed to the presence of enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes, which do not alter the shape of the high pressure abdominal aorta (this despite the fact that lymphoma is a leading cause of superior vena cava obstruction). The ureters can get caught up in the fibrosis at around L4/5 and become ectatic in their course. Bilateral medial deviation of the ureters is classical. Abnormal peristalsis and gradual tapering of the ureters is also seen.

On MRI fibrosis of any kind is usually low in signal and this is no exception. High signal on T2 can occur due to accompanying inflammation in some cases.

IgG4 related disease

IgG4 related diseases are one of Radiology’s newest entities. They comprise a constellation of fibrotic conditions affecting virtually every part of the body, mediated by a subclass of Immunoglobulin called IgG4. Where one condition exists others may also be present. The more common of these include:

Orbital pseudotumour

Fibrosing mediastinitis

Reidel thyroiditis

Autoimmune pancreatitis

Sclerosing mesenteritis

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

Retrocaval ureter

This congenital anomaly occurs almost exclusively in the right ureter only. Patients can be asymptomatic or present with right sided obstructive symptoms or recurrent urinary tract infections. On a urogram the course of the right ureter runs medially over the L3/4 pedicle and passes behind the inferior vena cava before returning to its normal course.

stem: You are performing a trans-vaginal ultrasound scan on a lady who presented to her GP with vague abdominal pains and constipation worsening over the last few months. In the left adnexal region there is a multilocular lesion measuring 8cm in diameter. No solid components are seen, there is no appreciable blood flow within it and no ascites.
prompt: According to the IOTA rules, how should this lesion be classified?
explanation:
This example could be a mucinous cystadenoma.

IOTA rules (International Ovarian Tumour Analysis)

In comparison to many other cancers, ovarian cancer has a relatively poor prognosis, partly on account of the vague nature of symptoms leading to presentation but also due to the limitations of diagnosis by ultrasound (often the first line of investigation for patients who end up being diagnosed with ovarian cancer).

The IOTA rules were designed to standardise ultrasound findings in ovarian lesions.

Two sets of rules were drawn up; M-rules and B-rules (indicating malignant and benign characteristics respectively). The rules have been designed to be as simple as possible, for general use by anyone capable of performing transabdominal or transvaginal imaging of the ovaries.

Malignant = One or more M-rule, no B-rules

Benign = One or more B-rules, no M-rules

Indeterminate = everything else

| B-rulesM-rulesB1 = Unilocular cystM1 = Solid, irregular massB2 = <7mm solid componentM2 = AscitesB3 = Acoustic shadow M3 = >3 papillary structuresB4 = Multilocular cyst <10cmM4 = Multilocular solid mass >10cmB5 = No blood flowM5 = Blood flow |
| --- |

Ovarian cancer

There are a number of different types of ovarian carcinoma and the final diagnosis will be a histological one. On imaging the features can be varied.

| Subtypes | Frequency and Age |
| --- | --- |
| Malignant epithelial tumours (Serous, mucinous, endometroid, clear cell) | 85% (60s -70s) |
| Malignant germ cell tumours (Teratoma, dysgerminoma, choriocarcinoma, mixed) | 7% (<30 years) |
| Metastases | <10% |
| Sex cord stromal tumours | ~5% |

A number of factors increase the risk of developing ovarian cancer in an individual. Anything which increases the number of ovulatory cycles a woman undergoes in her lifetime will increase the risk of ovarian cancer (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity), and vice versa (multiparity, breastfeeding, oral contraceptive pill use). A family history of related cancers also increases the risk.

Presenting symptoms may be quite vague with abdominal pains, constipation or urinary frequency being the only complaints if any from the patient. Consequently, many tumours have already spread beyond the ovary by the time of diagnosis. Initial investigation is often with ultrasound. Although ovarian cancers can have a variety of imaging appearances, solid or papillary components to a cystic mass are strongly indicative of malignancy. Predominantly solid masses with some small cystic components are also likely to be malignant but completely perfectly solid lesions are actually more likely to be benign. Ovarian fibromas and fibrothecomas are both benign lesions which can be seen as solid masses however despite this, without prior imaging for comparison a solid ovarian lesion is malignant until proven otherwise.

Ovarian cancer can spread in a multitude of ways:

| Direct extension | Sigmoid mesocolon, broad ligament, fallopian tubes |
| --- | --- |
| Intraperitoneal seeding and implantation | Omental caking, peritoneal space |
| Lymphatic spread | External iliac, obturator nodes |
| Haematogenous | Liver, lung, adrenal glands, pleural effusion |

Bowel obstruction is relatively common with disseminated ovarian cancer however it is usually large bowel obstruction. Small bowel obstruction is far less common.

stem: An 81-year-old man is undergoing pre-operative assessment prior to a routine TURP procedure for some troublesome lower urinary tract symptoms. When his PSA is found to be markedly elevated he undergoes an MRI scan for further investigation. A 12mm tumour is seen in the left peripheral zone. It returns low signal on the T2 weighted sequences, with low signal on the DWI sequence too. Dynamic contrast enhancement analysis reveals a type 3 curve.
prompt: Which of the following accurately describes this? Select ONE answer only.
options: A double peak wash in phase
A rapid wash in and subsequent washout phase
An increasing intensity with a long plateau phase
An initial plateau followed by a long washout phase
explanation:
From the findings on DWI described in the vignette it is not possible to tell if this is a PIRADS 3 or 4 lesion. Axial dynamic contrast enhanced imaging (after non-contrast axial T1) is essential to differentiate between between PIRADS 3 and 4 lesions. The three types of curve are known as type 1-2 curves. Type 3 curves are considered most suspicious for prostate cancer. Just like for breast cancer contrast enhancement curves, in a metabolically active lesion there is usually rapid uptake and rapid washout of contrast, leading to the classical type 3 curve. Type 1 and 2 curves in prostate imaging can also occur in malignant lesions but type 3 curves are the most concerning.

PIRADS curves © Medical Exam Prep

The assessment of peripheral zone and central zone lesions is very different in PIRADS assessment.

Peripheral zone

The highest grade of suspicion for malignancy in the peripheral zone is indicated by the presence of marked restricted diffusion (focal high b-value and corresponding low ADC signal), with a PIRADS 5 lesion being one that is greater than 1.5 cm. PIRADS 3 lesions will show some restricted diffusion but this is far less (subjective analysis) than for PIRADS 4 lesions. Dynamic contrast enhancement is used for assessment of peripheral zone lesions only - differentiating between lesions which show only limited restricted diffusion. If there is dynamic contrast enhancement with a type 3 washout curve, the lesion becomes a PIRADS 4 lesion despite the only limited restriction in diffusion.

Transitional zone

The highest grade of suspicion for transitional zone lesions is reserved for moderate T2 lesion which is lenticular or non-circumscribed and moderately T2 hypointense (PIRADS 5 >1.5 cm).

Three plane T2 imaging is common practice and enables full assessment of the peripheral zone of the prostate, particularly examining for extra-capsular extension, bladder base or seminal vesical invasion. T2 is also the most important sequence for lesions in the transitional zone.

Diffusion weighted imaging is essential for PIRADS calculation and is the first sequence that should be used to evaluate lesions in the peripheral zone.

The T1 weighted sequences are also useful to check for the presence of any haemorrhagic foci although since most patients now undergo their MRI scan prior to any biopsies being taken this has become far less important.

Interestingly the ADC map is more sensitive for carcinoma of the prostate (in the peripheral zone) than the DWI sequences. A finding of focal low signal on the ADC map may be seen in the absence of a corresponding high DWI focus. In the transitional zone however, the T2 sequences are more sensitive.

stem: A 63-year-old man undergoes a CT scan for investigation of weight loss. Several small, poorly defined, solid lesions are seen in the kidneys which enhance less than the renal parenchyma on the portal venous phase. There is evidence of widespread metastatic disease elsewhere on the study and it is suggested the renal lesions are likely to represent metastases.
prompt: Which of the following is the LEAST likely primary malignancy? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks for the LEAST likely option.

Metastases to the kidneys (although the 5th most common site of widespread malignancy) are usually a sign of end-stage metastatic disease and usually presents as multiple small renal masses. In colorectal cancer this can present as a single larger mass. Perinephric tumour is more suggestive of melanoma metastasis. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a relatively common cause of multiple renal metastases. Hodgkin lymphoma is generally confined to the lymph nodes and is a rare cause of renal metastases.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents with discomfort on passing urine following a gonococcal infection. He undergoes a retrograde urethrogram to further investigate. He is identified as having a stricture.
prompt: What is the most likely appearance of the stricture? Select ONE answer only.
options: Irregular long stricture of the distal bulbous urethra
Irregular stricture of the penile urethra
Short segment stricture of the bulbous urethra
Short segment stricture of the penile urethra
Smooth long segment stricture of the membranous urethra
explanation: Gonococcal infections classically cause long strictures. They are most commonly irregular in nature and located in the bulbous urethra. The distal bulbous urethra is most frequently affected.

stem: You are reviewing a scan in the gynaecology MDT. The patient is a 65-year-old lady who has recently been diagnosed with endometrial cancer following presenting to her GP with symptoms of post-menopausal bleeding.
prompt: Which of the following would provide the best information for staging her disease?
explanation:
Contrast is required for endometrial cancer staging in order to accurately assess the depth of myometrial invasion. Blood and blood degradation products are common features of uterine imaging and separating these from tumour is important. The tumours tend to enhance early, earlier than the endometrium, but to a lesser degree than the strongly enhancing myometrium. Images are usually taken at around 3-4 minutes post-contrast. Contrast images also help evaluate for invasion of the cervical stroma, a feature which carries the patient up to stage II if present. Contrast is also used in the staging of ovarian tumours but rectal tumours and cervical cancer are the pelvic tumours which do not use contrast for staging. The literature is divided as to whether it is useful for staging bladder cancers.

Endometrial cancer

Anything that increases unopposed oestrogen exposure causes an increased risk of endometrial cancer. For the most part it is a disease of the post-menopausal age group and thus presents with post-menopausal bleeding but around 10% of cases present prior to this with irregular bleeding. Initial investigation is often with ultrasound where any endometrial thickness of >5mm in a postmenopausal lady would be suspicious. <5mm of endometrial thickness has a 100% negative predictive value for endometrial carcinoma. Where there is a poorly defined interface between the endometrium and the myometrium, invasive carcinoma should be considered. Cellular diagnosis can be obtained at hysteroscopy , with dilatation and curettage or a pipelle biopsy.

| Phase | Days in cycle | Endometrial thickness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Menstrual | 1-7 | 1-4mm |
| Proliferative | 7-14 | 5-7mm |
| Periovulatory | 14 | 11mm |
| Secretory | 14-28 | 16mm |
| Post-menopausal | - | <5mm |

MRI is used for staging where it is the T2 weighted sequences which provide the most information. The myometrium and endometrium are separated by a black stripe called the junctional zone (aka transitional zone; the inner layer of myometrium). The endometrial cancer causes loss of the bright endometrial signal and breach of this black junctional zone denotes myometrial invasion. On T1 weighted images the layers are all isointense to one another. A crucial staging change comes with cervical invasion which denotes stage II. Fertility-sparing management (if required) is no longer a viable option and lymph node sampling is usually done at hysterectomy to detect any involved nodes which, if present, would upstage the patient to stage III. stem: A 32-year-old lady is being investigated for acute pelvic pain and fevers. She denies the possibility of a pregnancy since she uses an IUCD and indeed a b-hcg test is negative. Abnormalities on an ultrasound scan lead to further investigation with an MRI scan. This shows that she has a tubo-ovarian abscess.
prompt: What are the usual findings for a tubo-ovarian abscess on an MRI?
options: A complex pelvic mass with high T2 signal and anterior displacement of the broad ligament
A complex pelvic mass with low T2 signal and posterior displacement of the broad ligament
A simple tubular structure arising from the left adnexa with low T2 signal and thin enhancing walls
A tubular structure arising from the left adnexa with high T2 signal and thick enhancing walls
A tubular structure arising from the left adnexa with low T2 signal and thick enhancing walls
explanation:
Tuboovarian abscess (TOA)

A TOA can arise as a complication of PID. They therefore share the same aetiology of sexually transmitted infections, IUD insertion or pelvic surgery. They are ususally seen as a complex mass which encompasses the fallopian tube and ovary and it may not even be possible to accurately distinguish the anatomy of the fallopian tube or the exact location of the ovary within the mass. Unlike other pelvic abscesses a TOA usually forms posterior to the uterus, displacing the broad ligament anteriorly. Otherwise, imaging features are common to many other abscesses , namely a complex mass with thick enhancing walls and septae, and the liquid centre of which is low on T1 and high on T2 weighted sequences. They are often bilateral.

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)

This is a coverall term applied to ascending infection of the genital tract. It encompasses endometriosis, salpingitis, hydrosalpinx, pyosalpinx, and tubo-ovarian abscesses. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea account of most of the cases and the disease is most prevalent in sexually active young people. Imaging features are those secondary to inflammation with increased vascularity to the endometrium and small volume ascites. Inflammation is also seen on MRI as avid enhancement post contrast. Pelvic inflammatory disease can be complicated by a condition called Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome where there is perihepatitis secondary to PID.

Hydrosalpinx - A simple tubular structure with thin enhancing walls

Fluid within the fallopian tube is referred to as a hydrosalpinx. This can occur as a complication of endometriosis or PID and will be seen on imaging as a fluid-filled adnexal structure, distinct from the ovary. The walls are most often thin. On MRI the signal characteristics will depend on the protein content of the fluid but usually they are watery and therefore are low in signal on T1 and high in signal on T2.

Pyosalpinx -  A tubular structure with thick enhancing walls

A pyosalpinx can be seen within a TOA or can exist as a separate entity in its own right but the presence of a pyosalpinx does not completely stretch to a diagnosis of a TOA. Thick enhancing walls around an identifiably tubular adnexal structure are typical. Signs of surrounding inflammation may be seen too. The content usually has intermediate or high signal on T1 owing to the protein content of the pus and usually high signal on T2.

stem: A 20-year-old man attends a urology outpatient clinic having failed initial therapies for the management of his dysuria. He is scheduled for a cystoscopy which is normal and undergoes an MRI of the pelvis. This shows a Mullerian duct cyst.
prompt: Which of the following features is useful in differentiating a Mullerian duct cyst from a utricle cyst in this patient? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Anatomy plays a strong role in the correct diagnosis of male genitourinary tract cysts. It is first necessary to differentiate between intraprostatic cysts and extraprostatic cysts.

Mullerian duct cyst (intraprostatic)

These are usually found in young adult men and are also caused by incomplete regression of the Mullerian duct. They have numerous similarities with prostatic utricle cysts, including an association with renal agenesis (although not with intersex disorders). Anatomically they are also posterior to the bladder however unlike prostatic utricle cysts they extend superiorly to the prostate and do not communicate with the urethra. On MRI they appear straightforwardly cystic unless complicated by infection. The shape of the cyst is said to be teardrop shaped rather than the pear-shaped prostatic utricle cysts.

|  | Mullerian duct cyst | Prostatic utricle cyst |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Age | 20-40 years | 0-20 years |
| Shape | Teardrop | Pear |
| Extends above prostate? | Yes | No |
| Communicates with prostatic urethra? | No | Yes |

Prostatic utricle cyst (intraprostatic)

These are found in teenagers or adolescents and represent incomplete regression of the Mullerian duct system during embryological development. They are found posterior to the bladder, within the prostate, and do not extend any more superiorly than the superior most aspect of the prostate. This anatomical detail and the fact that the cyst does communicate with the prostatic urethra sets it apart from a Mullerian duct cyst on imaging. They can cause all manner of lower urinary tract symptoms and boast an association with ipsilateral renal agenesis as well as intersex disorders. On MRI they are said to have a pear-shaped appearance.

stem: An 18-month-old boy is referred for ultrasound after his parents noticed a lump in the right hemiscrotum. His serum aFP is raised. An ultrasound demonstrates a markedly enlarged testicle without a focal mass. Further imaging is performed which demonstrates multiple lung metastases.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Lymphoma

Testicular lymphoma is classically seen in an older man with bilateral hypoechoic lesions.

Teratomas, Yolk sac tumours, Embryonal cell tumours and Choriocarcinomas all fall into the category of Non-seminomatous Germ Cell tumours. Of these, Embryonal cell tumours make up the vast majority.

Teratoma

This is the second most common tumour in boys under 5. aFP is usually normal. Under ultrasound it appears as a heterogenous complex mass.

Yolk sac tumour

This makes up 80% of childhood testicular tumours.This can often present as testicular enlargement without a focal mass. It metastases to lung which is the most common site of recurrent disease.

Embryonal cell tumour

This is the second most common testicular tumour. It is the most aggressive of all testicular tumours with visceral metastases common and 5 year survival of 30%.

Choriocarcinoma

This is a rare tumour affecting 20-30-year-olds with rapid metastases to lung, liver, GI tract, brain. Often causes haemorrhage in both primary and metastatic lesions. Causes gynaecomastia in 10% due to raised serum hCG.

In reality, tumours are often mixed histological types (around 35% cases). Testicular tumours can also be diagnosed with a strong pre-test probability based solely on age as detailed in the table below. In reality, the role of the radiologist however does not need to be as complex as suggesting the final histological diagnosis. Establishing the presence of a testicular mass is sufficient. Patients should then be referred on to the urology MDT. On ultrasound there will be an intratesticular low reflectivity well-defined mass. Colour doppler flow can be seen within the mass.

| Age at diagnosis | Tumour |
| --- | --- |
| 10s | Yolk sac tumour or teratoma |
| 20s and 30s | Choriocarcinoma |
| 30s | Embryonal cell carcinoma |
| 40s | Seminoma |

stem: A 32-year-old woman becomes anuric, having initially recovered well, following a cadaveric renal transplant for the management of her polycystic kidney disease. You have been asked to perform an ultrasound scan on the transplanted kidney to confirm a diagnosis of renal vein thrombosis.
prompt: Which of the following findings would you expect to allow you to make the diagnosis?
explanation:
An increased resistive index is a sensitive finding for the presence of pathology but it is relatively non-specific.

Renal vein thrombosis

Transplant kidneys are most likely to develop renal vein thrombosis within their first week. Clinically the patient will become anuric with a tender and swollen kidney. Ultrasound is the mainstay of diagnosis and can show thrombus within the renal vein, however the diagnosis is usually made on the basis of the Doppler findings. Since the outflow from the kidney is obstructed the resistive index (the difference in velocity between systole and diastole divided by the systolic velocity) will increase to above 0.7. The resistive index, however, is not specific as it also increases in renal artery stenosis. Furthermore the arterial waveform changes and there may even be reversal of end-diastolic flow in the renal artery. This is seen as inversion of the colour Doppler trace.

Renal artery stenosis

There are three main aetiologies of renal artery stenosis. The most prevalent is atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is the second most common and is classically given as affecting a relatively young woman with beading (string of beads) of the mid and distal renal arteries seen, for which the management is angioplasty. Finally a small number of cases are secondary to a variety of conditions such as Buerger’s disease, Takayasu’s disease and neurofibromatosis.

The significance of diagnosis of atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis is in avoiding the use of ACE inhibitors. The ASTRAL trial showed that there was no long term benefit of stenting the stenoses over best medical management, although there was still a reduction in the number of episodes of flash pulmonary oedema experienced by the patients.

Slightly different numbers are given in the different sources.

| Signs of renal artery stenosis |  |
| --- | --- |
| Peak systolic velocity (PSV) | >150-180 cm/s |
| Ratio of peak renal artery velocity to peak aortic velocity (RAR) | >3.5 |
| Resistive Index (RI) | >0.7 |
| Difference in RI between left and right | >5% |
| Renal-interlobar ratio (RIR) | >5 |
| Pulsus parvus (increased peak) et tardus (late) waveform | - |

stem: A 78-year-old lady visits her GP with symptoms of weight loss and abdominal distension. On examination there is shifting abdominal dullness and the GP is suspicious for an ovarian malignancy. She refers the patient for an ultrasound scan.
prompt: Which of the following ultrasound features would be most suspicious for an ovarian malignancy?
explanation: Solid or papillary components to a cystic mass are strongly indicative of malignancy. Predominantly solid masses with some small cystic components are also likely to be malignant but completely perfectly solid lesions are actually more likely to be benign. Ovarian fibromas and fibrothecomas are both benign lesions which can be seen as solid masses however despite this, without prior imaging for comparison a solid ovarian lesion is malignant until proven otherwise.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
options: Adenocarcinoma of the gland of Skene
explanation: Malignant urethral lesions usually present in the 6th-7th decades and are more common in women than men. Urothelial carcinoma (also known as transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common however squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma are also found.

stem: You are performing a trans-vaginal ultrasound scan on a lady who presented to her GP with vague abdominal pains and constipation worsening over the last few months. In the left adnexal region there is a unilocular lesion with a solid mural component measuring 9x16mm. There is some slight colour doppler flow within the solid component, no acoustic shadow and no ascites.
prompt: According to the IOTA rules, how should this lesion be classified?
explanation:
The lesion is indeterminate because there are both M and B-rules.

B1 - unilocular

M5 - blood flow

IOTA rules (International Ovarian Tumour Analysis)

In comparison to many other cancers, ovarian cancer has a relatively poor prognosis, partly on account of the vague nature of symptoms leading to presentation but also due to the limitations of diagnosis by ultrasound (often the first line of investigation for patients who end up being diagnosed with ovarian cancer).

The IOTA rules were designed to standardise ultrasound findings in ovarian lesions.

Two sets of rules were drawn up; M-rules and B-rules (indicating malignant and benign characteristics respectively). The rules have been designed to be as simple as possible, for general use by anyone capable of performing transabdominal or transvaginal imaging of the ovaries.

Malignant = One or more M-rule, no B-rules

Benign = One or more B-rules, no M-rules

Indeterminate = everything else

| B-rules | M-rules |
| --- | --- |
| B1 = Unilocular cyst | M1 = Solid, irregular mass |
| B2 = <7mm solid component | M2 = Ascites |
| B3 = Acoustic shadow | M3 = >3 papillary structures |
| B4 = Multilocular cyst <10cm | M4 = Multilocular solid mass >10cm |
| B5 = No blood flow | M5 = Blood flow |

Ovarian cancer

There are a number of different types of ovarian carcinoma and the final diagnosis will be a histological one. On imaging the features can be varied.

| Subtypes | Frequency and age |
| --- | --- |
| Malignant epithelial tumours (Serous, mucinous, endometroid, clear cell) | 85% 60s -70s |
| Malignant germ cell tumours (Teratoma, dysgerminaoma, choricarcinoma, mixed) | 7% <30 years |
| Metastases | <10% |
| Sex cord stromal tumours | ~5% |

A number of factors increase the risk of developing ovarian cancer in an individual. Anything which increases the number of ovulatory cycles a woman undergoes in her lifetime will increase the risk of ovarian cancer (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity), and vice versa (multiparity, breastfeeding, oral contraceptive pill use). A family history of related cancers also increase the risk.

Presenting symptoms may be quite vague with abdominal pains, constipation or urinary frequency being the only complaints if any from the patient. Consequently many tumours have already spread beyond the ovary by the time of diagnosis. Initial investigation is often with ultrasound. Although ovarian cancers can have a variety of imaging appearances, solid or papillary components to a cystic mass are strongly indicative of malignancy. Predominantly solid masses with some small cystic components are also likely to be malignant but completely perfectly solid lesions are actually more likely to be benign. Ovarian fibromas and fibrothecomas are both benign lesions which can be seen as solid masses however despite this, without prior imaging for comparison a solid ovarian lesion is malignant until proven otherwise.

Ovarian cancer can spread in a multitude of ways:

| Spread of ovarian cancer |  |
| --- | --- |
| Direct extension | Sigmoid mesocolon, broad ligament, fallopian tubes |
| Intraperitoneal seeding and implantation | Omental caking, peritoneal space |
| Lymphatic spread | External iliac, obturator nodes |
| Haematogenous | Liver, lung, adrenal glands, pleural effusion |

Bowel obstruction is relatively common with disseminated ovarian cancer however it is usually large bowel obstruction. Small bowel obstruction is far less common.

stem: Arterial supply of the kidneys
prompt: The segmental branches of the renal artery divide to form which arteries? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The arterial supply to the kidneys is from the renal arteries, two fast flowing arteries that arise from the abdominal aorta at the L2 vertebral level. As the abdominal aorta is situated slightly to the left of the midline the right renal artery is longer than the left. The kidneys receive approximately 20% of the cardiac output.

After arising from the aorta, the right renal artery passes behind the inferior vena cava, the right renal vein, the head of the pancreas, and the second part of the duodenum as it travels to the kidney. The left renal artery passes behind the left renal vein, the body of the pancreas and the splenic vein as it travels to the kidney. The left renal artery is crossed anteriorly by the inferior mesenteric vein.

The renal arteries then enter the kidney at thehila of the kidneys, which lie approximately in the transpyloric plane at the L1 vertebral level. At the hila the renal arteries divide into four or five segmental branches.

Each segmental branch divides to form the interlobar arteries that are situated on either side of every renal pyramid. These interlobar arteries then undergo further division to form the arcuate arteries.

The interlobular arteries are then given off at right angles from the side of the arcuate arteries, and head into the cortical substance. Once within the cortex a final division takes place with the interlobular arteries dividing to form the afferent arterioles.

In the outer two-thirds of the cortex, the efferent arterioles form the peritubular network. The inner third of the cortex is supplied by long, straight arteries known as the vasa recta.

The interlobular arteries are then given off at right angles from the side of the arcuate arteries, and head into the cortical substance. Once within the cortex a final division takes place with the interlobular arteries dividing to form the afferent arterioles.
In the outer two-thirds of the cortex, the efferent arterioles form the peritubular network. The inner third of the cortex is supplied by long, straight arteries known as the vasa recta.

stem: A 42-year-old man with known type 2 diabetes mellitus undergoes an intravenous urogram following an acute admission with right sided ureteric colic. The IVU shows an egg-in-cup appearance with ‘tracks and horns’ in some of the calyces on the right mentioned in the report. The renal cortical thickness is normal and the left kidney is normal too.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal papillary necrosis

The point at which the collecting ducts in the medulla converge to become a minor calyx is known as the renal papilla. The renal papilla marks the beginning of transitional epithelium; hence transitional cell carcinoma can occur within the upper tracts. The papillae are vulnerable to ischaemia of any cause. The blood supply to the papillae is via end vessels ostensibly supplying either the medullary vasa recta or small and tortuous calyceal vessels. Despite this dual supply, both sources are primarily for other purposes and the renal papilla can suffer the consequences of insufficiency of any cause. Some of the predominant causes of renal papillary necrosis can be remembered with the mnemonic POSTCARDS.

| Causes of renal papillary necrosis |
| --- |
| Pyelonephritis |
| Obstruction |
| Sickle Cell Disease |
| Tuberculosis |
| Cirrhosis |
| Analgesic use |
| Renal vein thrombosis |
| Diabetes Mellitus |
| Systemic vasculitides |

Much of the damage and that which is demonstrable on imaging is explained by necrosis and sloughing off of the papilla to a greater or lesser extent. Signs such as tracks and horns, the lobster claw sign, signet ring sign or ball on a tee sign were originally described on IVU studies but translate reasonably well to CT urogram studies too. Filling defects within the collecting system occur when a papilla is complete sloughed off. These can go on to cause obstruction and hydronephrosis. The long term sequelae of renal papillary necrosis is calcification of the damaged papilla. The appearance is classically a garland pattern i.e. Many small or medium sized foci which appear to run in a line around the collecting system, at the junction of the pyramids and the collecting system.

Medullary sponge kidney

Dysplastic dilatation of the intramedullary collecting ducts permits urinary stasis which in turn promotes stone formation. Medullary Sponge Kidney is one of the main differential diagnoses for renal calcification. A quarter of cases are unilateral. This condition can be asymptomatic and noted incidentally or patients can be complicated by recurrent urinary tract infections, recurrent ureteric calculi or haematuria. The two main conditions seen in association with medullary sponge kidney are the collagen disorder Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Caroli disease which causes cystic dilatation of the intrahepatic biliary ducts. On imaging there are characteristic ‘Aunt Minnie’ type appearances when medullary calcification can be seen on a plain abdominal radiograph. Ultrasound shows increased echogenicity to the renal pyramids even in the absence of medullary calcification. On an IVU the appearance of the dilated ducts is often described to be like a bouquet of flowers or a bunch of grapes and is sometimes termed a ‘medullary blush’.

Urinary tract calculi

Ureteric colic is common and urinary tract calculi are even more so. There are many metabolic disorders which increase the risk of developing urinary tract calculi but many patients do develop calculi without any underlying cause. Stones can obstruct at any point along the urinary tract however the three narrowest points which are most liable to obstruction are the pelviureteric junction (PUJ), the vesicoureteric junction (VUJ) and at the point where the ureters cross the pelvic brim. As the ureter peristalses a characteristic extremely severe ‘loin-to-groin’ pain is experienced. A CT KUB study is a low dose, non-contrast, exam designed specifically to investigate for urinary tract calculi. A standard CT abdo/pelvis confers three times as much radiation dose at the very least. Although A CT KUB has a very high sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of opaque urinary tract calculi it is distinctly suboptimal for the evaluation of other causes of abdominal pain. Unfortunately since its introduction it has become a popular request for many a supposed loin-to-groin pain presentation.

| Stone composition | Associations and features | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcium oxalate/phosphate | Metabolic disorders, hyperparathyroidism or incidental | 75% |
| Struvite/matrix (MgPO3) | UTIs (acute and chronic especially Proteus), staghorn | 10-15% |
| Uric acid | Hyperuricaemia, gout, incidental. Can be seen on CT but not on AXR | 6% |
| Cysteine | Renal tubular defect | 1-2% |
| Indinavir phosphate | HIV medication, filling defects on urograms, not seen on CT or AXR | <1% |

Hyperparathyroidism

Parathyroid hormone acts to increase calcium levels either by promoting reabsorption in the kidneys or by acting on the osteoclasts of the bones and leads to increased bone resorption. This is seen as generalised osteopenia and cortical thinning, particularly of the subperiosteal bone.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is usually caused by an autonomous adenoma (alternatively parathyroid hyperplasia or a parathyroid carcinoma). Medullary nephrocalcinosis is most commonly caused by primary hyperparathyroidism but does also occur with secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a hyperplastic response of the parathyroid glands to the high phosphate and low calcium levels which accompany renal osteodystrophy. Soft tissue calcification is very much a feature of renal osteodystrophy. Confusingly the high circulating levels of phosphate in renal osteodystrophy leads to dystrophic mineralisation of trabecular bone which is seen as sclerosis; hence renal osteodystrophy is a cause of generalised increase in bone density despite hyperparathyroidism being a cause of osteopenia.

Tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs when a patient with secondary hyperparathyroidism (i.e. chronic overstimulation of the parathyroid glands) goes on to develop an autonomous adenoma.

stem: A GP practice nurse visits an 86-year-old poorly controlled diabetic Indian gentleman at his home. When she arrives he is clearly unwell; feverish and complaining of right upper quadrant pain. While she is visiting he experiences a rigor. She sends him to A&E where he undergoes an abdominal x-ray. This shows gas bubbles in the right hypochondrium. An ultrasound shows intrarenal and perirenal hyperechoic stranding.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Emphysematous Pyelonephritis

The radiological appearances of this condition are very striking, particularly on CT where streaky or lobulated gas can be seen in the renal parenchyma and perirenal tissues. On ultrasound the gas causes ring-down artefacts and is sometime described as giving a ‘dirty shadowing’ appearance. It is a very important diagnosis to make since it comes with significant morbidity. E-coli is the usual culprit and a history of poorly controlled diabetes is usual. The main differential diagnoses is the far less severe condition of emphysematous pyelitis where e-coli infection is confined to the excretory system and responds well to antibiotic therapy, and the presence of a fistulous connection to the bowel.

Malakoplakia

Directly translated from Greek, malakoplakia just means soft plaques. These are actually submucosal inflammatory plaques consisting of basophilic PAS positive inclusion bodies and incompletely destroyed e-coli bacteria. The giveaway pathological term is Michaelis-Gutmann inclusion bodies which are the incompletely destroyed e-coli bacteria surrounded by a lipoprotein membrane. Although malakoplakia can occur in anyone, patients with diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression are predisposed to it. Importantly though, it is not a pre-malignant condition unlike leukoplakia. On imaging there are filling defects in the bladder and distal ureters. These are usually small, measuring only a few millimetres across.

Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP)

This curious condition results from chronic pyelonephritis and leads to a non-functioning kidney. Chronic infection (most commonly with Proteus or e-coli) induces a granulomatous process whereby the renal tissue eventually becomes replaced by a mass of reactive tissue. Since proteus infection is one of the main causes it is not surprising that many cases present with a staghorn calculus. The exact association varies from 30-90% depending on the data source. The other finding on CT is of multiple low attenuation rounded areas with Hounsfield Units (HU) of around -15 to -20. These are the dilated calyces filled with debris and xanthoma collections and they cause the whole kidney to be enlarged. The appearance is said to resemble a bear’s paw. Patients can present either on a background of recurrent UTIs or potentially renal colic. Vague malaise and weight loss may be the presentation in the absence of direct urinary symptoms.

Renal tuberculosis

In areas of the world endemic to tuberculosis, renal tuberculosis is a reasonably common presentation of extra-pulmonary disease. The appearances on imaging vary depending on the disease timeline. The classical ‘putty kidney’ of renal tuberculosis is an end-stage appearance where there is dystrophic calcification affecting all parts of the kidney. At this point the kidney has usually become shrunken and small and the final appearance is of so-called autonephrectomy when there is essentially no parenchymal tissue left, just amorphous calcification. An earlier manifestation is stenosis to the infundibuli connecting the calyces to the renal pelvis causing proximal dilatation of the calyces which are seen to be clubbed on a urogram. Purportedly, the earliest sign is of moth-eaten calyces owing to uneven erosion to the papillae.

Leukoplakia

Directly translated from Greek, leukoplakia just means white plaques. It is a squamous metaplastic condition affecting the transitional cell epithelium of the bladder. Presentation is usually as a consequence either of recurrent urinary tract infections or urinary tract calculi. Sometimes patients complain of passing flaky white tissue in the urine which is pathognomonic for this condition. On imaging there is mucosal thickening and filling defects within the bladder. Some sources consider leukoplakia to be a premalignant condition for epidermoid carcinoma.

stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted with acute abdominal pain. He is hypotensive and tachycardic but sufficiently stable for a CT scan which shows a large retroperitoneal haematoma and a low attenuation lesion within the kidney. He is taken for embolisation and, on entry, the initial angiogram demonstrates microaneurysms within the lesion.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Angiomyolipoma (AML)

These are benign tumours which occur within the kidney and characteristically contain fat on CT scan. On an MRI scan they return high signal on both T1 and T2 and classically show signal drop-out on gradient echo sequences. They are usually small and harmless but occasionally can bleed into the retroperitoneum causing haemorrhagic shock (Wunderlich syndrome). This is more likely to occur the larger the AML due to the presence of microaneurysms. Those > 4 cm can be considered for resection or embolisation. Tuberous sclerosis is strongly associated with multiple angiomyolipomata which can be both large and numerous. Other phakomatoses such as Neurofibromatosis type 1 (not type 2) and von Hippel Lindau are also associated with AMLs to a lesser degree, as is polycystic kidney disease.

Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC)

Bladder TCCs are very common but renal TCCs less so. Nonetheless they have a knack for appearing in multiple locations at once and thus careful evaluation of the upper tracts is necessary each time a new diagnosis of bladder TCC is made. They appear as filling defects on the excretory phase of a CT scan or IVU.

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)

This is an ‘also-ran’ malignancy of the urinary tract accounting for 1% of kidney tumours. Clinically it will present in a similar fashion with haematuria however on CT there is no mass lesions to be seen as the SCC infiltrates the renal parenchyma causing renal enlargement with preservation of the overall kidney shape.

Oncocytoma

Oncocytomas have a characteristic feature of a stellate spoke wheel vascular pattern with an enhancing central scar. In reality there is so much overlap between the features of these tumours, which are largely benign, and renal cell carcinomas, that oncocytomas must be resected for histological confirmation of the diagnosis. They can present at any age but are usually asymptomatic, despite often being very large. In the real world they can engulf the perinephric fat and confusingly come to resemble an AML which is unhelpful.

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC)

This is the most common kidney tumour, accounting for around 80%. Patients are usually in their 50-70s although there is an increased incidence in dialysis patients and those with von Hippel Lindau. Clinically there is a classically macroscopic haematuria. A quarter or patients develop a paraneoplastic syndrome such as:

Hypercalcaemia

Polycythaemia due to erythropoietin

Stauffer syndrome (hepatomegaly without hepatic metastasis)

Limbic encephalitis

A renal protocol CT is used to evaluate lesions found on ultrasound and includes an unenhanced phase, a 60 second (corticomedullary) phase, and a 100 second (nephrogenic) phase. An excretory phase at 15 minutes can also be performed if evaluation of the collecting system anatomy is required (e.g. if the patient is a candidate for a partial nephrectomy). There are a number of different histological subtypes which are simplified and summarised in the table below:

| Histology | Prevalence | Associations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear cell renal carcinoma | 75% | Von Hippel Lindau syndrome |
| Papillary renal cell carcinoma | 15% | Most strongly associated with dialysis patients. Better prognosis than clear cell (if diagnosed prior to metastasis). |
| Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma | 5% | These are histologically like oncocytomas. Associated with Birt-Hogg-Dube (rare autosomal dominant disease affecting skin follicles, also causes lung cysts). They are thought to have a better prognosis than clear cell renal carcinoma. |
| Medullary carcinoma | <1% | Sickle Cell Trait |

stem: An 55-year-old man presents for an ultrasound scan with a left testicular lump. The ultrasound scan demonstrates hypoechoic masses in both testicles. Recent routine screening has shown an abnormally elevated PSA.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The differential diagnosis for bilateral testicular masses is reasonably short. Lymphoma is the most likely cause, especially in men aged over 60. Sarcoidosis is also a common cause of this uncommon finding. Leukaemia is difficult to differentiate from lymphoma on imaging alone and the two are usually discussed in tandem. Testicular metastases are themselves rare, but most common in patients over the age of 50 and the primary site is most commonly prostate or lung.

Lymphoma and leukaemia

Testicular lymphoma is uncommon but important. In men over the age of 60 it is the most common testicular malignancy and in men of any age it is the most common bilateral testicular malignancy (although it is not always bilateral). On ultrasound it appears either as a diffusely hypoechoic and enlarged testicle or as multiple hypoechoic masses.

The finding of a germ cell tumour, or bilateral ones, would be unusual at this age, though not impossible.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a long-standing history of haemoptysis presents to his GP complaining that recently he has been feeling very weak and generally unwell. His blood pressure is 170/110 mmHg with a heart rate of 70 bpm. Pulse oximetry shows his oxygen saturations to be 97%. He undergoes some basic blood tests and a CXR which shows bilateral lower zone consolidation with perihilar alveolar shadowing. His kidney function tests show him to be in renal failure.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Goodpasture syndrome

This is an autoimmune disease caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies. The alveolar membrane also falls victim to circulating auto-antibodies. Patients present as adolescents or young adults with glomerulonephritis and haemoptysis. Bilateral consolidation changes, especially in the perihilar regions, can be seen on imaging which characteristically become reticular over the ensuing few weeks. This is due to organisation of the pulmonary haemorrhage and can appear as a crazy paving pattern.

Granulomatous Polyangiitis (Previously termed Wegener granulomatosis)

This is an autoimmune vasculitis of the small and medium sized vessels. Patients present as young adults with glomerulonephritis and haemoptysis. On the face of it therefore there are strong similarities to Goodpasture syndrome). Chest imaging shows cavitatory nodules and the CT halo sign is considered characteristic. A giveaway feature is a raised c-ANCA level. Much like Goodpasture syndrome imaging is of limited diagnostic use as far as the renal manifestations are concerned.

Polyarteritis Nodosa

This is a necrotising vasculitis of small and medium sized vessels. There is an association with the hepatitis B and HIV viruses but otherwise patients present with vague symptoms of myalgia, fever, weight loss and high blood pressure.

stem: A 39-year-old man complains to his GP of a non-specific abdominal pains which have been getting worse over a period of around four months. Following numerous investigations he eventually undergoes a CT scan which shows very large metastatic nodal masses in the retroperitoneum and mediastinum. He undergoes a scrotal ultrasound which shows a tiny hypoechoic lesion in the left testis.
prompt: What is the most likely primary nature of the testicular lesion?
explanation:
Azzopardi tumour also known as a burnt out germ cell tumour

The primary tumour in these cases is a germ cell tumour which has outgrown its own blood supply and then regressed. Before doing so however it has metastasized to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes which can become extremely large. stem: The rectovesical fascia
prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the rectovesical fascia is true?
options: It is situated at the highest part of the rectovesical pouch
It plays an important role in limiting the spread of prostatic cancer
It separates the bladder from the vagina in the female
It separates the rectum from the kidneys in the male
It separates the rectum from the ovaries in the female
explanation:
The rectovesical fascia, which is also referred to as Denonvillier’s fascia, is a membranous partition situated at the lowest part of the rectovesical pouch.

In the male it separates the rectum from the prostate and urinary bladder (rectoprostatic fascia). In the female it separates the rectum from the vagina (rectovaginal fascia).

It plays an important role in limiting the spread of carcinoma, a classic example being the inhibition of the posterior spread of prostatic adenocarcinoma.

stem: A man presents for an ultrasound scan with a left testicular lump. The ultrasound scan demonstrates a 4cm heterogenous mass within the left testicle. Some cystic areas are seen within the mass. The referring clinician reports that the serum hCG is elevated. A chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar enlargement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Cystic areas within a testicular mass are commonly seen in non-seminomatous germ cell tumours. Teratomas, yolk sac tumours, embryonal cell tumours and choriocarcinomas all fall into the category of non-seminomatous germ cell tumours. Of these, embryonal cell tumours make up the vast majority.

Sarcoidosis is part of the differential diagnosis for bilateral testicular masses. Although bilateral hilar lymph node enlargement does fit with sarcoidosis, the elevated hCG does not.

Choriocarcinoma

This is a rare tumour affecting 20-30-year-olds with rapid metastases to lung, liver, GI tract, brain. They often causes haemorrhage in both primary and metastatic lesions. They cause gynaecomastia in 10% of patients due to raised serum hCG.

Lymphoma and leukaemia

Testicular lymphoma is uncommon but important. In men over the age of 60 it is the most common testicular malignancy and in men of any age it is the most common bilateral testicular malignancy (although it is not always bilateral). On ultrasound it appears either as a diffusely hypoechoic and enlarged testicle or as multiple hypoechoic masses.

Testicular leukaemia has very similar appearances to lymphoma and may be difficult to differentiate from it.

Teratoma

This is the second most common tumour in boys under 5. aFP is usually normal. Under ultrasound it appears as a heterogenous complex mass.

Yolk sac tumour

This makes up 80% of childhood testicular tumours. They can often present as testicular enlargement without a focal mass. These metastasize to the lung which is the most common site of recurrent disease.

Embryonal cell tumour

This is the second most common testicular tumour. It is the most aggressive of all testicular tumours with visceral metastases being common and a 5 year survival of 30%.

In reality, tumours are often mixed histological types in around 35% cases. stem: A 25-year-old presents with discomfort on passing urine. He previously sustained a straddle injury to his perineum following a bicycle accident. He undergoes a retrograde urethrogram to further investigate. He is identified as having a stricture.
prompt: What is the most likely appearance of the stricture? Select ONE answer only.
options: Irregular long stricture of the distal bulbous urethra
Irregular stricture of the penile urethra
Short segment stricture of the bulbous urethra
Short segment stricture of the penile urethra
Smooth long segment stricture of the membranous urethra
explanation:
Traumatic stricture

A previous traumatic straddle injury classically gives a short segment stricture of the bulbous urethra. In a straddle injury, the urethra is compressed against the pubic symphysis, often from a bicycle crossbar. A gonococcal infection causes a long, irregular stricture of the distal bulbous urethra.

Iatrogenic stricture

These can form following instrumentation, including prolonged catheterisation. They tend to be longer and smoother than other types of stricture. They usually occur at the main pre-existing narrow areas of the membranous urethra, bladder neck and meatus.

Infectious stricture

Gonococcal infections classically cause long strictures. They are most commonly irregular in nature and located in the bulbous urethra. The distal bulbous urethra is most frequently affected.

Radiotherapy stricture

In patients receiving radiotherapy to the perineum for prostate cancer, a urethral stricture can be a late complicating feature, occurring around 1-2 years following treatment. The stricture usually occurs at the bulbomembranous portion of the urethra, just distal to the prostate itself. Patients who have previously undergone a TURP are at increased risk of developing a post-radiotherapy stricture. They will be seen as a smooth stricture on imaging.

stem: A 35-year-old lady is involved in an RTA. She is stabilised at the scene and evacuated via helicopter to the trauma centre where she undergoes an immediate trauma CT. This shows, among lesser injuries, that the left kidney has sustained significant trauma.
prompt: Which of the following on CT would indicate the most severe renal injury?
options: Laceration involving the left renal pelvis
Subcapsular haematoma of the left kidney
explanation:
The priorities as far as surgery are concerned are:

Haemostasis

Preserving renal viability

Any injury which threatens either of these is an indication for urgent intervention. A vascular pedicle injury provides a significant threat to the viability of the kidney.

Traumatic injuries to the kidneys are graded according to the depth of parenchymal damage.

| Grade I | Subcapsular haematoma, no laceration |
| --- | --- |
| Grade II | <1 cm deep laceration, not involving collecting system (ie no free urine), retroperitoneal renal haematoma |
| Grade III | >1 cm deep laceration, not involving collecting system |
| Grade IV | Laceration involving renal pelvis, vascular injury with contained haemorrhage, segmental infarction, expanding haematoma causing renal compression |
| Grade V | Shattered kidney, vascular avulsion. |
| Bilateral injuries | Add one grade (i.e bilateral Grade II injuries is a Grade III injury overall). |

stem: A 46-year-old woman undergoes a pelvic MRI to investigate suspected endometrial cancer. Several pelvic sidewall nodes are rounded but measures under 1cm in short axis.
prompt: Which feature on MRI is most suggestive of metastatic nodal involvement? Select ONE answer only.
options: High signal on the high b-value images
explanation: Questions on MRI are becoming more frequent in the 2A to reflect modern practice and an understanding of useful sequences and techniques is essential. Diffusion weighted imaging is being used more frequently to problem-solve in subcentimeter nodes and the presence of restricted diffusion within a node is a feature suspicious for malignancy. Normal lymph nodes can and do demonstrate restricted diffusion too but this effect tends to be more marked in pathological lymph nodes though there is some overlap between benign and pathological lymph nodes at the low end of the spectrum. Nevertheless, a lymph node which is found to be strongly restricting diffusion, even if it appears otherwise morphologically benign should be suspected to be involved.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is undergoing chemotherapy for metastatic renal cell carcinoma. A follow up scan is performed at six months which shows a new hyper-enhancing nodule in the middle of the index tumour.
prompt: Which of the following is the best management of this patient? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The patient has developed a vascular aberration within the lesion, as it breaks down following chemotherapy treatment.

Traditional chemotherapy regimes are seldom used for renal cell carcinoma. The mainstay of treatment is resection or ablation for non-metastatic lesions or newer agents such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors for metastatic renal cell carcinoma.

With the advent of newer chemotherapy agents, the simplistic view of tumour monitoring with CT has changed. It is no longer sufficient to go by tumour dimension alone to determine treatment response; the characteristics of the lesion must be interrogated. Enhancement is a strong indicator of malignancy, but care must be taken not to miss vascular aberrations which would obviously be managed very differently. Acute intralesional haemorrhage, as the tumour outgrows its blood supply, may be seen as a fluid-fluid level of layering blood but in the absence of this sign can be difficult to discern and should be confirmed with an MRI scan to look for high T1 signal.

Radiofrequency ablation is particularly useful for small (<5cm) exophytic lesions though the desired response can also be seen with larger endophytic ones and each case should be judged on its merits.

stem: A 63-year-old man undergoes a CT scan for investigation of weight loss. Several small, poorly defined, solid lesions are seen in the kidneys which enhance less than the renal parenchyma on the portal venous phase. There is evidence of widespread metastatic disease elsewhere on the study and it is suggested the renal lesions are likely to represent metastases.
prompt: Which of the following is the LEAST likely primary malignancy? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks for the LEAST likely option.

Metastases to the kidneys (although the 5th most common site of widespread malignancy) are usually a sign of end-stage metastatic disease and usually presents as multiple small renal masses. In colorectal cancer this can present as a single larger mass. Perinephric tumour is more suggestive of melanoma metastasis. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a relatively common cause of multiple renal metastases. Hodgkin lymphoma is generally confined to the lymph nodes and is a rare cause of renal metastases.

stem: A 20-year-old man attends a urology outpatient clinic having failed initial therapies for the management of his dysuria. He is scheduled for a cystoscopy which is normal and undergoes an MRI of the pelvis. This shows a pear shaped cystic lesion posterior to the bladder. A distinct communication with the urethra is present. On the scout images the left kidney is notably absent.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anatomy plays a strong role in the correct diagnosis of male genitourinary tract cysts. It is first necessary to differentiate between intraprostatic cysts and extraprostatic cysts.

Prostatic utricle cyst (intraprostatic)

These are found in teenagers or adolescents and represent incomplete regression of the Mullerian duct system during embryological development. They are found posterior to the bladder, within the prostate, and do not extend any more superiorly than the superior most aspect of the prostate. This anatomical detail and the fact that the cyst does communicate with the prostatic urethra sets it apart from a Mullerian duct cyst on imaging. They can cause all manner of lower urinary tract symptoms and boast an association with ipsilateral renal agenesis as well as intersex disorders. On MRI they are said to have a pear shaped appearance.

Mullerian duct cyst (intraprostatic)

These are usually found in young adult men and are also caused by incomplete regression of the Mullerian duct. They have numerous similarities with prostatic utricle cysts, although the latter is associated with other congenital anomalies whereas Mullerian duct cysts are, classically, not. Anatomically they are also posterior to the bladder however unlike prostatic utricle cysts they extend superiorly to the prostate and do not communicate with the urethra. On MRI they appear straightforwardly cystic unless complicated by infection. The shape of the cyst is said to be teardrop shaped rather than the pear shaped prostatic utricle cysts.

|  | Mullerian duct cyst | Prostatic utricle cyst |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Age | 20-40 | 0-20 |
| Shape | Teardrop | Pear |
| Extends above prostate | Yes | No |
| Communicates with prostatic urethra | No | Yes |

Seminal vesicle cyst (extraprostatic)

Seminal vesicle cysts form due to stenosis or atresia of the ejaculatory ducts and can be post-infective in nature or congenital. They tend to present in adolescence due to the increase in secretions around this time. Acquired cysts are seen later on in life. The signal characteristics on MRI are variable depending on the presence or absence of haemorrhage. Anatomically it should be easy to pinpoint their location as relating to the seminal vesicles, namely posterior to the bladder and superior to the prostate. Congenital seminal vesicle cysts are associated with renal anomalies and adult polycystic kidney disease.

Urachal cyst (extraprostatic)

The urachus is a fibrous remnant of a thin canal connecting the bladder to the umbilicus. Ordinarily it is almost imperceptible however there are four distinct anomalies which can persist into adulthood and cause symptoms.

Patency – a fistula between the bladder and the umbilicus. There is leakage of urine from the umbilicus present from birth.

Sinus – blind dilatation of the urachus at the umbilical end.

Diverticulum – communication with the dome of the bladder

Cyst – dilatation in the lower third which does not communicate with either end. These are asymptomatic unless or until the cyst becomes infected or ruptures.

Malignancy arising from the urachas, unlike most bladder cancer, tends to be adenocarcinoma. In young patients sarcomas are also seen.

Cystic prostate cancer

Carcinoma of the prostate does not usually present as a cystic mass but the presence of haemorrhage within a cystic mass should raise the possibility of malignancy. Most prostate cancer arises from the peripheral zone and is seen as low T2 signal with restriction of diffusion. Cystic prostate cancer will return high signal on T2. The main differential diagnosis is a prostatic abscess.

stem: A 72-year-old man is undergoing pre-operative assessment prior to a routine TURP procedure for some troublesome lower urinary tract symptoms. When his PSA is found to be markedly elevated he undergoes an MRI scan for further investigation. A 12mm tumour is seen in the left peripheral zone. It returns low signal on the T2 weighted sequences, with some very low signal on the ADC sequence too.
prompt: Which of the following most accurately describes the role of PSA density? Select ONE answer only.
options: It contributes to both PIRADS and TNM scores
It gives the likelihood of cancer being present
It is an indication of the likely response to chemotherapy
explanation:
The PSA is usually considered elevated when levels exceed 4ng/L. A number of things can artificially elevate the PSA and in many cases of an incidental elevated PSA once these have been excluded the PSA returns to normal. Patients should be counselled to avoid activities which could lead to an elevated PSA for at least 48hrs prior to the test.

| False positive PSA | False negative PSA |
| --- | --- |
| 'Stradle' activities (bike riding, horse riding etc.) | Aspirin |
| Ejaculation | NSAIDs |
| Urinary tract infection |  |
| Prostatitis |  |
| Digital rectal examination |  |
| Benign prostatic hyperplasia |  |

The PSA density is calculated by taking the PSA and dividing it by the volume of the prostate. The volume is calculated as: Height x Length x Depth x π/6 (the volume of an ellipsoid). It accounts for the increase in size of the prostate which occurs in many men with increasing age and allows a far more comparable indication of the likelihood of malignancy. 0.1 is considered a normal PSA density value. Prostate cancers are usually seen in those with a prostate density of >0.1ng/ml/cc.

If a radiologist is reviewing a scan for a patient with a PSA density >0.1 and is unable to identify a prostatic malignancy then either they should review the scan more closely, or the PSA value could be repeated following appropriate instructions to the patient regarding cessation of PSA elevating activities prior to the test.

If a radiologist is reviewing a scan for a patient with a PSA density >0.1 and is unable to identify a prostatic malignancy then either they should review the scan more closely, or the PSA value could be repeated following appropriate instructions to the patient regarding cessation of PSA elevating activities prior to the test.

stem: You are reporting a CT abdomen and pelvis of a 68-year-old gentleman which shows a small exophytic mass arising from the lower pole of the right kidney.  You suspect this to be a renal cell carcinoma. There is no renal vein invasion or sign of local spread but you have noticed a mass in the left adrenal gland. It is 3.5cm in diameter and measures -15 Hounsfield Units on the unenhanced images and shows moderate enhancement on the portal venous phase.
prompt: What should you suggest?
explanation:
Despite the fact that this lesion has such low Hounsfield Units it demonstrates moderate enhancement and the patient has an existing malignancy.

| Known malignancy | No known malignancy |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0-3cm | >80% benign | 4-6cm | >70% malignant |
| >3cm | >80% malignant | >6cm | >80% malignant |

The best test to diagnose this lesion would be a dedicated adrenal CT scan (unenhanced, portal venous and 15 minute delayed phases). This would enable the radiologist to calculate the absolute and relative washout figures for the mass. The theory is that malignant lesions have greater permeability and therefore retain contrast for longer, giving lower washout values. By contrast benign adrenal adenomas will wash out faster, giving higher washout values.

Of the answers given an MRI scan of the adrenals would be best. An adrenal biopsy is invasive should only be sought if the combination of MRI and CT adrenal scans cannot fathom the answer. An MIBG scan is useful to look for an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma.

Adrenal adenoma

These present a diagnostic challenge if only to rule out a malignant adrenal mass. Once the diagnosis is confirmed they can then be left alone and do not require any further imaging. The majority are obvious on CT and obviously adenomas. Owing to their high fat content most adenomas show low Hounsfield units (HU) and HU <18 on an unenhanced study has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity approaching 100%.

In cases where the fat content is insufficient to make the diagnosis an adrenal protocol CT can be performed. This compares the HU on an unenhanced scan, a portal venous phase scan and a 15 minute delayed phase scan. From these values the absolute washout can be calculated by comparing the difference between the two contrast studies with the amount of contrast taken up in the first place (i.e. the difference between the portal venous phase and the unenhanced phase). The relative washout is calculated by comparing the difference between the two contrast studies to just the portal venous phase (i.e. it is relative to the portal venous phase).

An alternative diagnostic strategy which, but for demand management, is better for patients as far as dose preservation is concerned, is an MRI scan. The fat content of adrenal adenomas shows up well as signal loss on out-of-phase imaging and gives a chemical shift artefact in the frequency encoding direction on both gradient echo and spin echo sequences.  On gradient echo sequences due to the chemical shift a black line appears in all directions and is termed the India Ink effect or etching artefact.

| Diagnostic of adrenal adenoma |
| --- |
| At least 60% absolute washout |
| At least 40% relative washout |
| <18 HU (99% specific) |
| <37 HU on a delayed scan |
| India ink effect on GE MRI |
| Chemical shift on GE and SE MRI |

Adrenal metastasis

This is an important differential diagnosis for a malignant lesion of the adrenal gland. Lung cancer is the most obvious culprit but other cancers do also metastasize to the adrenal glands (Breast, Colorectal, Renal cell, Malignant melanoma, Pancreas). Metastases take on a variety of appearances depending on their cell type but usually retain contrast for longer than adenomas leading to low washout figures. Owing to their neoplastic nature they are however, usually reasonably vascular and therefore show strong enhancement in the portal venous phase (>100HU). On an MRI scan they enhance with gadolinium but importantly fail to show any signal loss on fat suppression sequences.

stem: A 45-year-old lady presents with right flank pain. She denies any history of trauma. She undergoes a CT scan which demonstrates a 5 cm fat-dense lesion within the right kidney. The radiologist also notes an 8mm tubular structure in the right flank with surrounding fat stranding.
prompt: Which of the following would be the most accurate description of this clinical presentation? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
This patient has appendicitis and an incidental large AML. Following treatment for her acute presentation she should receive counselling for the risk of AML rupture and be offered prophylactic embolisation.

Wunderlich syndrome

Spontaneous haemorrhage/rupture is a known complication of AMLs and is termed Wunderlich syndrome. Patients with AMLs larger than 4cm are at particularly increased risk of this. Wunderlich syndrome can occur in the context of Tuberous Sclerosis or in a patient with an isolated large AML. Although Wunderlich syndrome is most commonly caused by an underlying AML, it can also be seen with renal cell carcinoma or vascular malformations.

Tuberous sclerosis

This condition would explain the presence of a fat containing renal lesion (if it wasn't simply a sporadic finding) but has no relation to the dilated and inflamed appendix. Not all patients with tuberous sclerosis have AMLs and not all of those with AMLs have large enough ones to rupture, and not all of those with large AMLs experience Wunderlich syndrome.

Majewski Syndrome

This is a variant of short-rib polydactyly syndrome with no renal associations.
