stem: A 39-year-old man complains to his GP of a lump in his scrotum. He is referred for an ultrasound which shows that there is an anechoic unilocular lesion at the head of the epididymis which shows posterior acoustic enhancement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Epididymal cyst

A cystic structure within the epididymis is most commonly a simple cyst. They can present as palpable masses or be found incidentally. On ultrasound they behave as you might expect from a cyst, with posterior acoustic enhancement of an anechoic round structure. The main differential diagnosis is a spermatocoele which, unlike a simple cyst, usually contains echogenic material. The latter is usually only found in the epididymal head.

Spermatocoele

A spermatocoele is a focal dilatation of a duct within the head of the epididymis. Since they contain protein debris and spermatozoa, low level echoes can be seen floating within them differentiating them from epididymal cysts. They are essentially an incidental asymptotic finding.

Rete testis ectasia

This is a relatively common finding in men around the age of 60. It is asymptomatic and therefore incidental. The rete testis is the name given to the tubules which collect spermatozoa from the seminiferous tubules and deliver them to the extra-testicular ducts. The normal rete testis is too small to appreciate with ultrasound but when, through age, the distal portion becomes stenosed, there is buildup of fluid within the rete testis. This is then seen as tubular branching anechoic structures within the testis.

Tunica albuginea cyst

The tunica albuginea is a fibrous layer covering the testicle. On ultrasound it appears as the thin echogenic line surrounding the testicle. When cysts form here they are usually palpable as small well-defined lumps a few millimetres in diameter. Appearances on ultrasound usually conform to those expected from any straightforward cyst i.e. An sharply defined anechoic structure with acoustic enhancement posteriorly. They can be uni or multilocular and although they can exert mass effect on the underlying testicle they do not affect the testicular tissue beyond this. They are most commonly located at the anterosuperior or superolateral aspect of the testicle.

Intratesticular cyst

These are not readily palpable and therefore are seen only as incidental findings. They demonstrate the usual characteristics of any cyst on ultrasound but are located within the testicle itself. They are inconsequential but for their distinction from cystic teratomas. The latter will have solid enhancing components on an MRI scan. Provided, however, there is no ambiguity on ultrasound, no further follow up would be needed for a straightforward intratesticular cyst.

Seminoma

Germ cell tumours are divided into seminomas and non-seminomatous varieties. They are very common and comprise almost half of all testicular tumours. They can often be found incidentally or subsequent to any trauma which might cause the patient to self-examine and discover a testicular lump. Alternatively they can present as a vague dull scrotal aching sensation with no lump.

Lymphatic drainage is to the retroperitoneum. Para-aortic lymph nodes are therefore regional. Involvement of the internal, external and common iliac nodes however, is considered non-regional. Only if there has been previous scrotal or inguinal surgery disrupting tissue planes are inguinal or external iliac artery nodes considered regional.

They typically are found in patients in their 40s. Testicular tumours can be diagnosed with a strong pre-test probability based solely on age as detailed in the table below. On ultrasound there will be an intratesticular low reflectivity well-defined mass. Colour doppler flow can be seen within the mass.

| Age at diagnosis | Tumour |
| --- | --- |
| 10s | Yolk sac tumour or teratoma |
| 20s + 30s | Choriocarcinoma |
| 30s | Embryonal cell carcinoma |
| 40s | Seminoma |

They can be uni or multilocular and although they can exert mass effect on the underlying testicle they do not affect the testicular tissue beyond this. They are most commonly located at the anterosuperior or superolateral aspect of the testicle.
Intratesticular cyst

These are not readily palpable and therefore are seen only as incidental findings. They demonstrate the usual characteristics of any cyst on ultrasound but are located within the testicle itself. They are inconsequential but for their distinction from cystic teratomas. The latter will have solid enhancing components on an MRI scan. Provided, however, there is no ambiguity on ultrasound, no further follow up would be needed for a straightforward intratesticular cyst.
Seminoma

Germ cell tumours are divided into seminomas and non-seminomatous varieties. They are very common and comprise almost half of all testicular tumours. They can often be found incidentally or subsequent to any trauma which might cause the patient to self-examine and discover a testicular lump. Alternatively they can present as a vague dull scrotal aching sensation with no lump.

Lymphatic drainage is to the retroperitoneum. Para-aortic lymph nodes are therefore regional. Involvement of the internal, external and common iliac nodes however, is considered non-regional. Only if there has been previous scrotal or inguinal surgery disrupting tissue planes are inguinal or external iliac artery nodes considered regional.

They typically are found in patients in their 40s. Testicular tumours can be diagnosed with a strong pre-test probability based solely on age as detailed in the table below. On ultrasound there will be an intratesticular low reflectivity well-defined mass. Colour doppler flow can be seen within the mass.

| Age at diagnosis | Tumour |
| --- | --- |
| 10s | Yolk sac tumour or teratoma |
| 20s + 30s | Choriocarcinoma |
| 30s | Embryonal cell carcinoma |
| 40s | Seminoma |

stem: An 81-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with left loin pain, fevers and rigors. Blood tests show he is septic. An ultrasound shows mild left sided hydronephrosis. He undergoes a CT KUB which confirms a 10mm proximal ureteric stone.
prompt: Which of the following would be best to manage this patient? Select ONE answer only.
explanation: This is one of those questions that tutors can devote whole sessions to debating and the reality of the situation is that in real life you might expect the most important management steps (antibiotics and nephrostomy) to take place concurrently. In an exam setting however we must simplify things to tease out the essence of the question. Since the patient is septic, the best management plan must be to combat that. Antibiotics are going to be crucial to the management of this patient but do not address the cause of the sepsis. A 10mm stone is highly unlikely to pass spontaneously.

stem: The ureters
prompt: Ureteric stones are most likely to become lodged in which of the following points? Select ONE answer only.
options: 2 cm distal to the renal hila
At the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries
At the inferior border of the transverse colon
At the level of the ischial tuberosities
Near the inferior pole of the kidney
explanation:
The ureters are two muscular ducts that carry urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder. They are usually 25-30 cm long and approximately 3-4 mm in diameter. They lie in the retroperitoneal space.

They arise from the pelvis of the kidney and exit at the hila in the transpyloric plane at the L1 vertebral level. From the hilum they run vertically downwards, passing along the anterior surface of psoas major. They cross the pelvic brim at close to the sacroiliac joints to enter the pelvic cavity. At this point the cross the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries.

Once within the pelvis they turn anteromedially at the level of the ischial spines, to head towards the bladder. Upon reaching the bladder they pierce its lateral aspect in an oblique fashion. This creates a valve that prevents the backflow of urine.

The ureters contain three points of constriction. These are important clinically as the most common sites for kidney stones to become lodged:

At the ureteropelvic junction of the renal pelvis and the ureter

As the ureter crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries to enter the pelvis

At the ureterovesical junction as the ureter obliquely enters the bladder

The ureter lies in close association with several important abdominopelvic viscera including the appendix, colon and ovaries. This places the ureter at risk from inflammatory, infectious, or malignant processes from these viscera and these can manifest as haematuria, pyuria, fistula, or obstruction. The mass effect of constipation, pregnancy, or ovarian cysts can cause ureteric obstruction.

Sensory input from the ureters travels to the T11-L2 levels of the spinal cord and can be referred to the corresponding dermatomes. Pain from the ureter, for example form ureteric colic, may therefore be referred to the posterior lumbar/flank region or the hypogastrium.

stem: A 67-year-old woman undergoes a CT scan of her adrenal glands for an incidental lesion picked up on a CT colonogram. The lesion is situated in the lateral limb of the left adrenal gland and is 2cm in diameter. It measures 38HU on the unenhanced sequence, 115HU on the portal venous phase and 75HU on the delayed sequences. You may use a calculator.
prompt: What is the absolute washout of this lesion?
explanation:
Figures have been rounded to the nearest whole number.

Absolute washout = (115-75)/(115-38) = 52%

Relative washout = (115-75)/115 = 35%

This lesion is non-adenomatous. Given the avid contrast enhancement on the arterial phase (>110HU) a phaeochromocytoma should be strongly suspected.

Adrenal washout

Washout characteristics of adrenal nodules help confirm or refute a diagnosis of an adrenal adenoma. The absolute washout takes into account the initial uptake of contrast whereas the relative washout calculation is based only on how well contrast washes out of a nodule.

The underpinning principle is that vasculature within malignant lesions is more permeable than in benign lesions. This allows contrast to diffuse out of the lesion during the portal venous phase and the contrast is then slower to wash out during the delayed phase than it would be for benign lesions. Thus the higher/faster washout characteristics (either absolute or relative) the more suggestive it is that a lesion is benign.

Phaeochromocytomas also known as adrenal paragangliomas.

Paragangliomas are found all over the body and called different things in different places despite the fact that the histology is the same.

Phaeochromocytomas are known as the 10% tumours. Purportedly 10% are: bilateral, asymmetrical, familial, are extra-adrenal, contain calcification. The most well known syndromic association is with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) type II (both a and b). They do also occur with phakomatoses (von Hippel Lindau, neurofibromatosis type I, Sturge Weber and Tuberous Sclerosis).

The classic but rare presentation is of uncontrollable hypertension due to catecholamine production and the classic giveaway blood test is elevated levels of urinary VMA.

On CT they can have a range of appearances including post-haemorrhagic or necrotic low attenuation, solid and/or cystic areas. They enhance strongly and are slow to washout. On MRI they tend to return low T1 signal (excepting areas of haemorrhage which may be high) but very bright T2 signal giving rise to the lightbulb sign. The main differential diagnosis would be of adrenal cortical carcinoma. Phaeochromocytomas don't invade the IVC and won't cause atrophy of the contralateral adrenal gland, where adrenal cortical carcinomas can.

MIBG scanning (I123-Metaiodobenzylguanidine)

This comes under the broader heading of a guanethidine analogue and can be used to pinpoint catecholamine producing tumours such as phaeochromocytomas or other paragangliomas. The scan can be used to locate an extra-adrenal phaeochromocytoma. The tracer is also taken up by neuroblastomas, carcinoid tumours and medullary carcinoma of the thyroid.

If the CT scan shows morphologically normal adrenal glands then an MRI scan is unlikely to be of any further benefit. A dedicated MRI scan of the adrenal glands with in and out of phase sequences might be useful in the setting of an indeterminate mass; if there is signal dropout within the mass it is likely to be an adenoma.

An adrenal biopsy should 'never' be performed for a suspected phaeochromocytoma. The risk is of provoking catecholamine release and triggering extreme hypertension or a cardiac arrhythmia.

stem: The kidneys
prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the kidneys is true?
options: The adrenal glands lie posterior to the kidneys
The hila lie at the T12 vertebral level
The right kidney lies posterior to the jejunum
The right kidney lies slightly lower than the left kidney
The subcostal nerves lie anterior to the kidneys
explanation:
The kidneys are two retroperitoneal organs that lie on the posterior abdominal wall. They are responsible for electrolyte and fluid balance and also for the filtration and excretion of waste products from the blood.

Each kidney lies on its respective side of the vertebral column between the T12 and L3 vertebral levels. The right kidney lies slightly lower than the left because of the presence of the large right lobe of the liver. The kidney moves during respiration, one particular study noted that the maximal vertical motion of the superior pole of the kidney from its end-expiratory to its end-inspiratory position is around 40 mm.

At the concave medial margin of each kidney is a vertical cleft called the renal hilum. This is the point where the renal artery and vein enter and exit the kidney respectively. The hila of the kidney lie approximately in the transpyloric plane at the L1 vertebral level.

The principal relations of each kidney are shown in the table below:

|  | Left kidney | Right kidney |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anterior relations | Left adrenal glandSpleenStomachPancreasLeft colic flexureJejunum | Right adrenal glandLiverDuodenumRight colic flexure |
| Posterior relations | Diaphragm11thand 12th ribsPsoas majorQuadratus lumborumTransversus abdominisSubcostal nerveIliohypogastric nerveIlioinguinal nerve | Diaphragm12th ribPsoas majorQuadratus lumborumTransversus abdominisSubcostal nerveIliohypogastric nerveIlioinguinal nerve |

The kidneys and their main relations (from Gray’s Anatomy)

stem: A 30-year-old man taking part in a mountain biking competition is injured in a crash and taken to hospital. He has obvious pelvic fractures and urethral trauma is suspected when blood is noted at the tip of the penile meatus. The surgical registrar believes he may have a bulbar urethral injury.
prompt: Which of the following is the most appropriate method of confirming this?
explanation:
A retrograde urethrogram is performed by inserting a catheter into the tip of the penis and injecting contrast. Pictures are then taken to show the entire length of the urethra with a small amount of contrast spilling into the bladder.

A retrograde urogram involves catheterisation of the ureters via a cystoscope. Images are then taken of contrast being injected to show the length of the ureters and renal collecting systems.

A micturating (or voiding) cystourethrogram is performed to investigate for reflux in children among other indications. The bladder is filled retrograde with contrast via a catheter and images are then taken of the bladder, ureters and urethra while the patient voids.

A CT urogram is performed as a delayed sequence approximately 15 mins after an IV injection of iodinated contrast. This gives time for some of the contrast to be filtered by the kidneys and opacify the ureters and bladder.

Saddle injuries

Although rarely life threatening, urethral injuries can cause significant morbidity in the long-term. A trauma CT may not pick up urethral injuries unless combined with some form of urethrography. Although the posterior urethra is most associated with blunt force ‘saddle’ injuries, the anterior urethra can also be injured in this way. Haematuria, blood visible at the penile meatus and a ‘high-riding’ prostate on digital rectal examination are all signs of a potential urethral injury.

Assuming the patient is sufficiently stable from any other injuries sustained (life threatening injuries must always take priority!), the initial management of urethral injuries relies on a high index of suspicion. Blind catheterisation should not be attempted if a urethral injury is suspected and the patient should go on to have urethral imaging as soon as feasible. An anterior urethral injury can be investigated for with retrograde urethrography initially, followed by a VCUG to look for any posterior urethral injuries.

| --- | --- |
| Less common (33%)The glandular, penile and bulbous urethraInjured in penetrating trauma, iatrogenic trauma or straddle injuriesLess commonly associated with pelvic fracturesInvestigate with retrograde urethrography | More common (67%)The prostatic and membranous urethraInjured in blunt trauma (straddle injuries)More commonly associated with pelvic fracturesInvestigate with a voiding/micturating cystourethrogram (VCUG) |

stem: A 35-year-old woman undergoes an abdominal ultrasound scan as part of work up for infertility. There is left sided hydronephrosis. She undergoes a CT KUB which shows no stones.
prompt: Which of the following would be best to manage this patient?
explanation:
The MAG3 scan will show whether the kidney is truly functionally obstructed.

MAG3

Dynamic scan. Images every 2 mins for approximately 20 mins

MAG3 is a compound which has a high renal extraction rate and can be labelled with Tc99m. It provides an overview of the renal plasma flow. A normal unobstructed kidney shows an initial increase in activity over 2 minutes as the tracer reaches the kidney followed by a slow decline in activity over around 20 minutes as it is filtered. An obstructed system will show a similar initial increase, but activity will then not decline. Furosemide can be given to maximise the opportunity to show flow distal to the kidney. MAG3 is a safe agent to use in patients with renal failure.

Captopril (an ACEi) can be given to diagnose renal artery stenosis as a cause of hypertension since the activity in a patient with renal artery stenosis will decline following administration of Captopril whereas a normal kidney will retain activity.

Post-micturition images at 20 minutes can help to show the presence of residual bladder volume.

DTPA – differential agent

Dynamic scan. Images at 1.5 second intervals for the first 30 seconds then less at 5 min intervals for 30 mins

Since DTPA is cleared only via the glomeruli it can be used to measure GFR. In a normal kidney the activity level peaks sharply followed by a decline which is initially rapid and then tapers off. As GFR worsens firstly the initial rapid decline becomes more gradual and with increasingly poor disease the initial peak then becomes diminished too. Ironically for a study used to measure GFR, DTPA is not a good agent for patients with renal failure; it can only be cleared via the glomeruli therefore if there is no glomerular filtration the agent will persist and lead to a high dose. Studies need higher doses than MAG3.

DMSA – morphology and structure

Static scan. Image once at 2 hours.

DMSA is an excellent agent for evaluating the renal cortex. It is used a lot in the paediatric setting in the investigation of scars following pyelonephritis.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a known malignancy undergoes a CT scan for suspected diverticulitis. As well as the diverticulitis, this demonstrates a 3 cm right adrenal lesion which has a mean attenuation of 28 Hounsfield Units.
prompt: What is the LEAST likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note the question asks for the LEAST likely diagnosis.

Even in a patient with a known malignancy, an adenoma is the most likely diagnosis. For adrenal metastases, lung malignancy is the most common malignancy which metastases to the adrenal glands, followed by breast, and then colon, stomach and melanoma. The adrenal glands are the 4th most common site of metastatic involvement with both glands involved 50% of the time.

stem: The breast
prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the anatomy of the breast is FALSE?
options: The axillary nodes drain approximately 30% of lymph from the breast
The axillary tail runs along the lateral edge of the breast
The breast lies superficial to serratus anterior
The nipple is mainly composed of smooth muscle fibres
Vertically the breast spans between the 2nd and 6th intercostal cartilages
explanation:
The breasts are paired structures lying on the anterior chest wall in the pectoral region. They are present in both males and females but become more prominent in the female following puberty. In females the breast contains the mammary glands, which are the key structures involved in lactation.

The breast typically extends horizontally from the lateral border of the sternum to the mid-axillary line. Vertically the breast spans between the 2nd and 6th intercostal cartilages. It lies superficially to both the pectoralis major and serratus anterior muscles.

The nipple lies at the centre of the breast and is mainly composed of smooth muscle fibres. A pigmented area of skin referred to as the areolae surrounds the nipple. There are numerous sebaceous glands within the areolae that enlarge during pregnancy. The large, prominent part of the breast is referred to as the circular body. A smaller part that runs along the inferior lateral edge of pectoralis major towards the axillary fossa is referred to as the axillary tail.

The lymphatic drainage of the breast is of great clinical importance due to its role in breast cancer metastasis. There are three groups of lymph nodes that receive lymph from breast tissue:

The axillary nodes – approximately 75% of the lymph from the breast travels to the ipsilateral axillary nodes

The parasternal nodes – approximately 20% of the lymph from the breast travels to the ipsilateral parasternal nodes

The posterior intercostal nodes – approximately 5% of the lymph from the breast travels to the posterior intercostal nodes

The skin of the breast drains into the axillary, inferior deep cervical and infraclavicular nodes. The nipple and areolae drain into the subareolar lymphatic plexus.

stem: A prostate MRI is performed for suspected prostate malignancy. The peripheral zone returns uniform high T2 signal. The reporting radiologist suspects there may be malignancy within the transitional zone.
prompt: Which of the following MRI features indicates the highest level of suspicious for a malignancy in the transitional zone? Select ONE answer only.
options: Avid early enhancement with rapid lesion washout
Focal high b-value and corresponding low ADC signal
Focal low b-value and corresponding high ADC signal
Lenticular focus of moderate T2 hypointensity
explanation:
The assessment of peripheral zone and central zone lesions is very different in PIRADS assessment.

Peripheral zone

Dynamic contrast enhancement is used for assessment of peripheral zone lesions only - differentiating between PIRADS 3 and 4 lesions. The highest grade of suspicion for malignancy in the peripheral zone is indicated by the presence of restricted diffusion (focal high b-value and corresponding low ADC signal), with a PIRADS 5 lesion being one that is greater than 1.5 cm.

Transitional zone

The highest grade of suspicion for transitional zone lesions is reserved for moderate T2 lesion which is lenticular or non-circumscribed and moderately T2 hypointense (PIRADS 5 >1.5 cm).

stem: You are performing a trans-vaginal ultrasound on a 27-year-old lady. She presented to A+E with severe acute pelvic pain and vomiting. She denies per vaginum bleeding and a beta-hcg test was performed which was elevated. The gynaecology registrar suspects she may have an ectopic pregnancy.
prompt: Which of the following is most specific for an ectopic pregnancy?
explanation:
A decidual cast refers to the appeance of echogenic debris within the uterine cavity in the context of an ectopic pregnancy. All the other signs also occur in an intra-uterine pregnancy.

Ectopic pregnancy

Vaginal bleeding is very common in early pregnancy but vaginal bleeding with pain or pain without vaginal bleeding definitely call for an ectopic pregnancy to be excluded. Factors which increase the risk of ectopic pregnancy include:

Previous ectopic

IVF conception

Previous surgery to the Fallopian tubes

stem: A 33-year-old lady being investigated for primary infertility is found to have a solitary ovarian lesion on transvaginal ultrasound scanning. It has an anechoic centre and demonstrates peripheral vascularity on colour Doppler flow. A βHCG urine test performed the same day was negative.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Corpus luteal cyst

The corpus luteum comprises the remnant of an ovarian follicle post ovulation. Without fertilisation the normal corpus luteum will involute spontaneously within 2 weeks but occasionally they can persist even in the absence of fertilisation and be seen as a corpus luteum cyst. Ultrasound characteristics depend slightly on the age of the cyst and the presence or absence of haemorrhage within it but a small (<3 cm) thick walled, rounded, cystic structure with peripheral vascularity (the so-called ‘ring of fire’) would be classical. A repeat ultrasound scan after 6 weeks (to ensure a different part of the menstrual cycle) is usually recommended.

Mature teratoma

Teratomas and dermoid cysts have very similar imaging characteristics despite their histological differences. Teratomas are the most common ovarian neoplasm but are slow growing and usually benign. By contrast immature teratomas are malignant. The presence of fat is a strong indicator for a mature teratoma with the combination of fat, fluid and calcification being highly specific. On MRI the fat will show the usual signal drop-out on gradient echo sequences. Calcification will show as low signal on T2. Although benign, mature teratomas can be complicated by torsion or rupture. Malignant degeneration if it does occur, is to squamous cell carcinoma most commonly.

Endometrioma

These occur as part of the spectrum of endometriosis. Although often ovarian in location they can be found in the peritoneal cavity as well as elsewhere. The ectopic endometrial tissue undergoes cyclical haemorrhage leading to a build-up of blood products and debris which gives rise to a variety of imaging characteristics. Most commonly they appear as a single cyst with posterior acoustic enhancement and homogeneous internal low-level echoes on ultrasound. On MRI the signal characteristics will vary depending on the blood content. High T1 signal suggests old blood products but must be differentiated from the fat of a potential teratoma by checking to see that the signal persists (or is not suppressed) on the fat saturated sequences. The presence of the Shading sign is very suggestive of an endometrioma and occurs when there is low signal on T2 as blood products are usually low on T2. The shading sign is useful to make the distinction from haemorrhagic corpus luteal cysts since the fresh blood in those will not have degraded sufficient to cause the T2 darkening of endometriomas.

Yolk sac tumour

These unpleasant germ cell tumours affect adolescents and can be quite large at presentation. A raised serum AFP is common. They are usually solid with or without cystic areas. Since they can arise from an ovarian dermoid, sometimes fat signal can also be seen in association with these tumours.

Leydig-Sertoli tumour

It would be unusual to find a Leydig-Sertoli tumour in a patient older than 30 and most patients are in their early teens. Normal Leydig and Sertoli cells are found in the testes and produce testosterone and oestrogen respectively, among other hormones. Leydig-Sertoli tumours often produce one or both hormones in excess leading to virilisation and amenorrhoea, although some patients may experience no hormonal manifestations. AFP is often elevated. They are solid, fibrous tumours which can show cystic elements where haemorrhage or necrosis has taken place. Owing to their fibrous nature they usually return low signal on MRI, with/without high signal foci related to the cystic areas.

stem: A 64-year-old lady attends her GP surgery complaining of dysuria and urinary frequency. It is her third urinary tract infection in the past 12 months. During a thorough history, her GP also establishes that she has been experiencing some post-menopausal bleeding. An ultrasound is requested and a left-sided ovarian thecoma is diagnosed.
prompt: Which of the following would be the most likely findings on ultrasound?
options: Endometrial hyperplasia with a unilateral cystic ovarian mass
Endometrial hyperplasia with a unilateral echogenic solid mass
Endometrial hyperplasia with a unilateral hypoechoic solid mass
No endometrial hyperplasia with a unilateral cystic ovarian mass
No endometrial hyperplasia with bilateral echogenic solid masses
explanation:
Thecoma

These fibrous tumours do secrete oestrogen and hence can lead to endometrial hyperplasia with post-menopausal bleeding since they occur in ladies of a more mature nature. On ultrasound they typically appear as hypoechoic but solid ovarian masses. Atypical appearances include heterogeneity or hyperechogenicity. Owing to their fibrous nature they tend to return low signal with both T1 and T2 weighting on MRI. Endometrial hyperplasia and potential consequent carcinoma should be evaluated for with both modalities.

stem: A 66-year-old man undergoes a CT scan of his adrenal glands for an incidental lesion picked up on a CT colonogram. The lesion is situated in the lateral limb of the left adrenal gland and is 2cm in diameter. It measures 21HU on the unenhanced sequence, 65HU on the portal venous phase and 50HU on the delayed sequences. You may use a calculator.
prompt: What is the absolute washout of this lesion?
explanation:
Figures have been rounded to the nearest whole number.

Absolute washout = (65-50)/(65-21) = 34%

Relative washout = (65-50)/65 = 23%

This lesion is non-adenomatous and the patient should be referred for PET/CT or resection depending on the clinical scenario. In many centres, if the lesion measures less than 10HU on the unenhanced sequence then the study will be terminated at that point.

Adrenal washout

Washout characteristics of adrenal nodules help confirm or refute a diagnosis of an adrenal adenoma. The absolute washout takes into account the initial uptake of contrast whereas the relative washout calculation is based only on how well contrast washes out of a nodule.

The underpinning principle is that vasculature within malignant lesions is more permeable than in benign lesions. This allows contrast to diffuse out of the lesion during the portal venous phase and the contrast is then slower to wash out during the delayed phase than it would be for benign lesions. Thus the higher/faster washout characteristics (either absolute or relative) the more suggestive it is that a lesion is benign.

stem: A 51-year-old lady complains to her GP of irregular vaginal bleeding. She is referred for a transvaginal ultrasound scan. This shows a thickened myometrium which cannot be distinguished from the endometrium. On colour Doppler imaging there is increased vascularity to the myometrium.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Adenomyosis and endometrial cancer can be hard to distinguish in some patients and both can show increased vascularity however in this question it is the myometrium which is thickened and pathological with possible extension to the endometrium rather than the other way around. Adenomyosis affects the myometrium whereas endometrial cancer arises from the endometrium.

Adenomyosis

Thought by some to be a variant on the theme of endometriosis, adenomyosis is the ectopic presence of endometrial tissue within the myometrium. Its presence also causes smooth muscle proliferation. Adenomyosis can occur either diffusely or be limited to a focal area. On an HSG there will be small diverticuli but on MRI the classical description is of widening of the transitional zone (aka junctional zone; the inner layer of myometrium) to greater than 12mm. Small areas of high T1 and T2 signal are seen representing areas of haemorrhage and cystic change respectively.

| Increased risk of endometrial cancer |
| --- |
| Iatrogenic oestrogens |
| Tamoxifen |
| Early menarche or late menopause |
| No children |
| PCOS |
| Obesity |
| Diabetes |

Endometrial cancer

Anything that increases unopposed oestrogen exposure causes an increased risk of endometrial cancer. For the most part it is a disease of the post-menopausal age group and thus presents with post-menopausal bleeding but around 10% of cases present prior to this with irregular bleeding. Initial investigation is often with ultrasound where any endometrial thickness of >5mm in a postmenopausal lady would be suspicious. <5mm of endometrial thickness has a 100% negative predictive value for endometrial carcinoma. Where there is a poorly defined interface between the endometrium and the myometrium, invasive carcinoma should be considered. Cellular diagnosis can be obtained at hysteroscopy , with dilatation and curettage or a pipelle biopsy.

| Phase | Days in cycle | Endometrial thickness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Menstrual | 1-7 | 1-4mm |
| Proliferative | 7-14 | 5-7mm |
| Periovulatory | 14 | 11mm |
| Secretory | 14-28 | 16mm |
| Post-menopausal | - | <5mm |

MRI is used for staging where it is the T2 weighted sequences which provide the most information. The myometrium and endometrium are separated by a black stripe called the junctional zone (aka transitional zone; the inner layer of myometrium). The endometrial cancer causes loss of the bright endometrial signal and breach of this black junctional zone denotes myometrial invasion. On T1 weighted images the layers are all isointense to one another. A crucial staging change comes with cervical invasion which denotes stage II. Fertility sparing management (if required) is no longer a viable option and lymph node sampling is usually done at hysterectomy to detect any involved nodes which, if present, would upstage the patient to stage III. Endometrial cancer spread via the lymph nodes can involve any of the pelvic lymph node groups (with the exception of inguinal nodes which are non-regional for endometrial cancer), and the para-aortic lymph nodes. Indeed the para-aortic lymph nodes can sometimes be enlarged in the absence of pelvic lymph node involvement so careful examination of all the lymph node groups must be performed.

Contrast is required for endometrial cancer staging in order to accurately assess the depth of myometrial invasion. Blood and blood degradation products are common features of uterine imaging and separating these from tumour is important. The tumours tend to enhance early, earlier than the endometrium, but to a lesser degree than the strongly enhancing myometrium. Images are usually taken at around 3-4minutes post-contrast. Contrast images also help evaluate for invasion of the cervical stroma, a feature which carries the patient up to stage II if present. Contrast is also used in the staging of ovarian tumours but rectal tumours and cervical cancer are the pelvic tumours which do not use contrast for staging. The literature is divided as to whether it is useful for staging bladder cancers.

The presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity is known as endometriosis. It can be a debilitating condition, causing significant pelvic pain and is a leading cause of subfertility. stem: A 45-year-old man presents for an ultrasound scan with a left testicular lump. The ultrasound scan demonstrates hypoechoic masses in both testicles. A chest x-ray performed for his dry cough also shows bilateral hilar enlargement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The differential diagnosis for bilateral testicular masses is reasonably short. Lymphoma is the most likely cause, especially in men aged over 60. Sarcoidosis is also a common cause of this uncommon finding. Leukaemia is difficult to differentiate from lymphoma on imaging alone and the two are usually discussed in tandem. Testicular metastases are most common in patients over the age of 50 and the primary site is most commonly prostate or lung.

Bilateral testicular abscesses could be a differential diagnosis however clinical correlation is key.

Lymphoma and leukaemia

Testicular lymphoma is uncommon but important. In men over the age of 60 it is the most common testicular malignancy and in men of any age it is the most common bilateral testicular malignancy (although it is not always bilateral). On ultrasound it appears either as a diffusely hypoechoic and enlarged testicle or as multiple hypoechoic masses.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is being investigated for chronic pelvic pain. She describes the pain as a dull ache which has been getting worse over the past 6 months. There is no cyclical pattern to the pain but she reports the pain to be worse on walking. She has no other symptoms but is very anxious that she may have a gynaecological malignancy. She has previously been very active and well with no prior gynaecological symptoms. She had three normal deliveries with her children and had no problems thereafter. An MRI scan has been performed and you are reviewing the images. There are no pelvic masses but you do see multiple serpiginous structures in the pelvis which are very low in signal on T1 weighted sequences and have a variable signal intensity on T2 weighted sequences.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pelvic congestion syndrome

There is controversy in the literature regarding this syndrome. It is considered by many to be a diagnosis of exclusion as a cause for pelvic pain and some regard it as the female equivalent to a testicular varicocoele.

There is a rich network of veins extending between the ovarian veins (draining to the left renal vein and vena cava respectively) and the uterine veins (draining to the internal iliac veins). Engorgement of these vessels is thought to lead to a non-cyclical dull aching pain which can worsen on walking and with postural changes. Pelvic congestion syndrome does arise idiopathically or can be as a result of obstruction at any point between the internal iliac vein and renal veins. Pelvic tumours may lead to vascular engorgement either by direct invasion and thrombosis of draining vessels or by extrinsic compression.

On MRI the dilated and tortuous vessels take on a serpiginous appearance with flow voids on the T1 weighted sequences explaining their lack of signal. Moving blood has a variety of different appearances on T2 weighted sequences. Gradient echo sequences will show very low signal.

May-Thurner syndrome

Compression of the left common iliac vein by the right common iliac artery as the one crosses the other at the level of the bifurcation produces symptoms of left leg swelling. Pelvic collateral vessels may develop as the blood attempts to divert around the obstruction.

Ovarian vein thrombosis

This usually presents as a complication following delivery. Patients complain of acute/subacute abdominal pain and the condition can be complicated by delayed diagnosis and septicaemia, as well as pulmonary emboli. Thrombosis can also occur in the setting of a pelvic tumour or as a complication of pelvic surgery.

stem: Renal architecture
prompt: Which of the following structures empties urine into the renal pelvis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The parenchyma of the kidney is divided into two major structures:

The outer renal cortex and;

The inner renal medulla

The renal cortex extends into the medulla and divides it into triangular shaped areas referred to as the renal pyramids. Each renal pyramid combines with the renal cortex above it to form a renal lobe. Between the renal pyramids are projections of renal cortex referred to as the renal columns.

The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron. These are responsible for the production of urine and span the cortex and medulla. The initial filtering portion of the nephron is the renal corpuscle, which is located in the cortex. This is followed by the renal tubule that extends into the renal pyramids. Within the renal cortex lies the medullary ray, which is a collection of renal tubules that drains into a single collecting duct.

At the apex of each renal pyramid is the renal papilla. This empties urine into the minor calyx. Several minor calices combine to form a major calyx. Urine drains from the minor calices into the major calyx and the empties into the funnel-shaped renal pelvis. Urine then drains from the renal pelvis into the ureter.

explanationBlocks.content: The parenchyma of the kidney is divided into two major structures:
The outer renal cortex and;
The inner renal medulla

The renal cortex extends into the medulla and divides it into triangular shaped areas referred to as the renal pyramids. Each renal pyramid combines with the renal cortex above it to form a renal lobe. Between the renal pyramids are projections of renal cortex referred to as the renal columns.

The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron. These are responsible for the production of urine and span the cortex and medulla. The initial filtering portion of the nephron is the renal corpuscle, which is located in the cortex. This is followed by the renal tubule that extends into the renal pyramids. Within the renal cortex lies the medullary ray, which is a collection of renal tubules that drains into a single collecting duct.

At the apex of each renal pyramid is the renal papilla. This empties urine into the minor calyx. Several minor calices combine to form a major calyx. Urine drains from the minor calices into the major calyx and the empties into the funnel-shaped renal pelvis. Urine then drains from the renal pelvis into the ureter.

stem: A 29-year-old lady presents with shortness of breath and tachycardia. A full blood count and renal function tests are normal, as is a chest radiograph. The admitting team suspect she may have a pulmonary embolism and the decision is taken to perform a CTPA study, in part due to tracer non-availability at the hospital. The clinical team asks what she should do about breast-feeding her 3-month-old daughter.
prompt: What should you advise? Select ONE answer only.
options: She should switch to formula feeding
explanation:
Considerations during lactation

Less than 1% of injected iodine or gadolinium is excreted into breast milk and less than 1% of this is then absorbed by the baby's intestinal tract. Although these amounts are considered acceptably low as to not necessitate any breast-feeding cessation advice many families are understandably over-cautious. It is accepted that contrast agents are undetectable in blood 24 hours after administration and so any mother wishing to 'pump-and-dump' despite the negligible risks need not do so for longer than a day. Care should, however, be given to counsel the family that it is possible for inadvertent weaning to occur even after short intervals and this should be factored in to any decision made by the family.

Following a nuclear medicine study the risks to the baby are two-fold; firstly from tracer excretion into the breast milk, but also through proximity to the mother during breast-feeding. Recommendations for breast-feeding interruption vary depending on the half-life of the tracer used. For perfusion imaging using technetium (half-life 6 hours) breast milk should be expressed for the first 24 hours following the scan. In theory, it need not be discarded but can safely be bottle-fed to the baby after these 24 hours have elapsed, however in practice many patients none-the-less choose to discard it.

Most tracers simply require adherence to a washout time but of note, the precautions following administration of Gallium-67 based tracers (most commonly used for pyrexia of unknown origin) are much more limiting and, practically speaking, unfortunately lead to complete cessation of breastfeeding. The half-life of Ga-67 is approximately 78 hours. Breastfeeding should, if time allows, be stopped for 2-4 weeks prior to the scan to allow the breast tissue to become less radiosensitive while the tracer circulates within the mother. Where this is an unacceptably long delay for the clinical state of the patient the study can be performed straight away anyway but in either case, milk should also be discarded for at least a further two weeks following the study. Clearly a disruption to breast-feeding of such a long time is far from ideal, even assuming that a patient who is sufficiently unwell as to need a PUO study is able to continue breast-feeding at all, and is likely to lead to complete cessation of breast-feeding. There are other ways to image PUO using Tc99m labelled white blood cells which can be considered.

Imaging in pregnant patients (for PE)

A pregnant patient suspected to have a pulmonary embolus should undergo a chest x-ray to look for alternative causes of shortness of breath such as a lower respiratory tract infection, pleural effusions or a pneumothorax. In the event that they go on to have a VQ scan a chest radiograph is required for comparison.

Thereafter the patient should undergo bilateral lower limb venous dopplers if they have signs or symptoms of deep vein thrombosis. Around a third of pregnant patients who develop pulmonary emboli will have a deep vein thrombosis and for these patients treatment can be started on the basis of their DVT diagnosis without the need for further imaging. If the patient has no signs or symptoms of a DVT, they should proceed to a VQ scan or a CTPA.

The patient should be counselled that there is a small increase in the absolute risk of the foetus developing a childhood cancer following a maternal VQ scan but also that the absolute risk of maternal breast cancer is reduced compared to a CTPA.

CTPA

CTPA imaging confers a lower dose to the foetus than V/Q scanning, although this effect is diminished in the third trimester as the gravid uterus becomes closer to the field of view.

Unfortunately however, CTPA confers a far greater dose to the breast tissue of the mothers at a time when the tissue is more radiosensitive than it would otherwise be in a non-pregnant woman.

A secondary consideration is the use of iodinated contrast. Iodine crosses the placenta and is excreted by the foetal kidneys into the amniotic fluid. Babies of mothers who have received iodinated contrast during pregnancy should be tested during their first week of life for thyroid suppression although there is little evidence in literature to suggest that many if any infants have developed hypothyroidism following maternal intravenous iodine exposure.

Technical factors to performing a CTPA scan in pregnant patients, if required, are also important to consider. Hyperdynamic circulation can render usual triggering bolus mechanisms suboptimal and raise the possibility of a non-diagnostic study.

V/Q or Q only scanning

V/Q scanning confers a far lower breast dose to the mother but the dose to the foetus, particularly when small, can be greater owing to tracer accumulation within the solid organs of the mother. The mother should be encouraged to adequately hydrate and void frequently in the subsequent hours/days following a scan.

Many institutes choose to perform perfusion scanning only in pregnant women on the understanding that if the perfusion scan is normal then there is no need to go on to perform the ventilation study. The perfusion scan can also be performed at half the usual dose to further reduce the foetal-dose. Naturally doing so comes with the trade-off of lower sensitivity and specificity.

Gadolinium in pregnancy

Gadolinium also crosses the placenta and is excreted by the foetus into the amniotic fluid. The chelated form of gadolinium in itself poses no risk to the foetus however the free form of gadolinium is teratogenic and the longer the foetus is exposed to the chelated gadolinium administered for the scan, the greater the risk of each molecule of gadolinium becoming dissociated from its chelate. For this reason therefore, gadolinium should only be administered in a patient known to be pregnant, if there is likely to be significant diagnostic benefit from the resultant images.

stem: A 40 -year-old woman presents with acute abdominal pain. On examination she is tender and pyrexial. She is pyrexial, with an elevated WCC/CRP. Imaging shows that she has an IUCD which is correctly positioned in the uterus, a right adnexal abscess which is tracking into the psoas, and right sided hydronephrosis.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Actinomycosis

The bacterium actinomyces israelii produces proteases which allows it to cross structures which would otherwise present a barrier to spread of infection. Within the abdominal cavity actinomycosis leads to abscess formation, and fistula development. It is usual for the patient to have previously suffered a ruptured appendix or to be using an IUCD, or other similar entities. In the case of an IUCD, tuboovarian abscesses can form and spread locally to involve the psoas. Extrinsic ureteric compression leads to hydronephrosis.

Tuberculosis

Abdominal tuberculosis most commonly affects the ileocaecal junction with thickening of the ileocaecal valve and narrowing of the terminal ileum. This can be seen on fluoroscopic examination as the Fleischner sign or umbrella sign where the gaping ileocaecal valve abuts the thin, strictured terminal ileum. Local lymph node enlargement with or without central low attenuation to the lymph nodes may be seen on CT. Multiple different lesions in multiple sites (i.e. skip lesions) is also a feature and a characteristic feature is of elevation of the margins of an ulcer which follow the orientation of lymphoid follicles. In the colon this means the margins are elevated in the transverse plane but in the terminal ileum they are longitudinal.

The involvement of the ileocaecal valve and the presence of skip lesions means that a key differential diagnosis is Crohn disease. Over half of cases of abdominal tuberculosis will have concurrent ascites whereas this is a relatively rare feature for Crohn disease and can be used as a discriminator.

Specifically relating to the stomach, tuberculosis can cause pyloric stenosis, multiple deep ulcers on the lesser curve, and linitis plastic type narrowing of the antrum.

stem: A 72-year-old man is undergoing pre-operative assessment prior to a routine TURP procedure for some troublesome lower urinary tract symptoms. When his PSA is found to be elevated he undergoes an MRI scan for further investigation. A 12mm nodule is seen in the left peripheral zone. It returns high signal on the T2 weighted sequences, with no restricted diffusion.
prompt: What is the PSA density most likely to be? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The PSA is usually considered elevated when levels exceed 4ng/L. A number of things can artificially elevate the PSA and in many cases of an incidental elevated PSA once these have been excluded the PSA returns to normal. Patients should be counselled to avoid activities which could lead to an elevated PSA for at least 48hrs prior to the test.

| False positive PSA | False negative PSA |
| --- | --- |
| 'Stradle' activities (bike riding, horse riding etc.) | Aspirin |
| Ejaculation | NSAIDs |
| Urinary tract infection |  |
| Prostatitis |  |
| Digital rectal examination |  |
| Benign prostatic hyperplasia |  |

The PSA density is calculated by taking the PSA and dividing it by the volume of the prostate. The volume is calculated as: Height x Length x Depth x π/6 (the volume of an ellipsoid). It accounts for the increase in size of the prostate which occurs in many men with increasing age and allows a far more comparable indication of the likelihood of malignancy. 0.1 is considered a normal PSA density value. Prostate cancers are usually seen in those with a prostate density of >0.1ng/ml/cc.

If a radiologist is reviewing a scan for a patient with a PSA density >0.1 and is unable to identify a prostatic malignancy then either they should review the scan more closely, or the PSA value could be repeated following appropriate instructions to the patient regarding cessation of PSA elevating activities prior to the test.

stem: A 19-year-old lady who, six months previously, returned from her gap year travelling around the world attends her GP surgery complaining that her urine is cloudy. She denies any history of dysuria or fevers but says she has been feeling generally tired and unwell recently. An MSU reveals 3+ of leucocytes with no nitrites present. A KUB ultrasound performed a week later is grossly abnormal and the patient is sent for an IVU. This shows there to be infundibular stenosis and calyceal clubbing to the right kidney. The left kidney is normal.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal tuberculosis

In areas of the world endemic to tuberculosis, renal tuberculosis is a reasonably common presentation of extra-pulmonary disease. The appearances on imaging vary depending on the disease timeline. The classical ‘putty kidney’ of renal tuberculosis is an end-stage appearance where there is dystrophic calcification affecting all parts of the kidney. At this point the kidney has usually become shrunken and small and the final appearance is of so-called autonephrectomy when there is essentially no parenchymal tissue left, just amorphous calcification. An earlier manifestation is stenosis to the infundibuli connecting the calyces to the renal pelvis causing proximal dilatation of the calyces which are seen to be clubbed on a urogram. Purportedly, the earliest sign is of moth-eaten calyces owing to uneven erosion to the papillae.

Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP)

This curious condition results from chronic pyelonephritis and leads to a non-functioning kidney. Chronic infection (most commonly with Proteus or e-coli) induces a granulomatous process whereby the renal tissue eventually becomes replaced by a mass of reactive tissue. Since proteus infection is one of the main causes it is not surprising that many cases present with a staghorn calculus. The exact association varies from 30-90% depending on the data source. The other finding on CT is of multiple low attenuation rounded areas with Hounsfield Units (HU) of around -15 to -20. These are the dilated calyces filled with debris and xanthoma collections and they cause the whole kidney to be enlarged. The appearance is said to resemble a bear’s paw. Patients can present either on a background of recurrent UTIs or potentially renal colic. Vague malaise and weight loss may be the presentation in the absence of direct urinary symptoms.

Malakoplakia

Directly translated from Greek, malakoplakia just means soft plaques. These are actually submucosal inflammatory plaques consisting of basophilic PAS positive inclusion bodies and incompletely destroyed e-coli bacteria. The giveaway pathological term is Michaelis-Gutmann inclusion bodies which are the incompletely destroyed e-coli bacteria surrounded by a lipoprotein membrane. Although malakoplakia can occur in anyone, patients with diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression are predisposed to it. Importantly though, it is not a pre-malignant condition unlike leukoplakia. On imaging there are filling defects in the bladder and distal ureters. These are usually small, measuring only a few millimetres across.

Leukoplakia

Directly translated from Greek, leukoplakia just means white plaques. It is a squamous metaplastic condition affecting the transitional cell epithelium of the bladder. Presentation is usually as a consequence either of recurrent urinary tract infections or urinary tract calculi. Sometimes patients complain of passing flaky white tissue in the urine which is pathognomonic for this condition. On imaging there is mucosal thickening and filling defects within the bladder. Some sources consider leukoplakia to be a premalignant condition for epidermoid carcinoma.

Schistosomiasis

Schistosoma larvae burrow through human skin and travel via the lymphatics to the lungs and liver to mature. Thence they continue onto the pelvic vessels where eggs are deposited in the bladder wall. There the eggs cause both a granulomatous and an inflammatory reaction which erodes through the bladder mucosa and the eggs are then excreted in the urine. The disease is endemic to many parts of Africa.

The dominant imaging feature is of bladder wall calcification. This is usually described as curvilinear or floccular and involves all of the layers of the bladder. Owing to the chronic fibrotic reaction the bladder eventually becomes restricted and small; thus the standout imaging feature is of a small calcified bladder. The main differential diagnosis of bladder wall calcification is tuberculosis.

Another important facet to these cases is the risk of bladder cancer developing in the context of chronic inflammation. These cancers are squamous cell carcinomas and should be actively looked for in cases of schistosomiasis; there is a latent period of approximately 20 years prior to development.

stem: A 55-year-old lady undergoes an ultrasound as part of assessment for a new lump in her right breast. The ultrasound shows a 1.5 cm hypoechoic mass with hyperechoic margins and a lobulated contour.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A mucinous carcinoma is a subtype of infiltrating/invasive ductal carcinoma. The ultrasound findings are those of many other suspicious lesions too however mucinous carcinoma is the only one which would fit best. Differentiating this from a different type of carcinoma would be difficult.

Mondor syndrome is inflammation of a vein in the skin overlying the breast or chest causing the vein to have a tender cord-like feeling on palpation. It is a self limiting condition with symptoms alleviated with NSAIDs.

A fibroadenoma would be typically in a younger patient in their 20-30s. These are largely hypoechoic with a range of additional features but can have an echogenic halo.

A galactocoele would appear cystic on ultrasound.

A breast abscess clinical manifestations notwithstanding, would also appear cystic on ultrasound.

stem: A 66-year-old smoker is admitted with worsening left flank pain. An ultrasound scan shows severe left sided hydronephrosis and dilatation of the proximal left ureter. He undergoes an IVU which shows filling defects in both proximal ureters including one at the point of obstruction on the left.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC)

Bladder TCCs are very common but renal TCCs less so. They can also occur in the ureters but also have a knack for appearing in multiple locations at once and thus careful evaluation of the upper tracts is necessary each time a new diagnosis of bladder TCC is made. They appear as filling defects on the excretory phase of a CT scan or IVU.

Predisposing factors include cigarette smoking as well as exposure to a number of chemical dye compounds. Presentation is most frequently with painless haematuria but presentations due to obstructive features are also seen.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of James Heilman, MD CC BY-SA 4.0

Local staging is best performed by MRI where the tumour will appear more hyperintense than skeletal muscle on T2 weighted sequences and the presence or absence of invasion of the detrusor muscle (which returns very little signal)  is easily discernible.

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)

This is an ‘also-ran’ malignancy of the urinary tract accounting for 1% of kidney tumours. Clinically it will present in a similar fashion with haematuria however on CT there is no mass lesions to be seen as the SCC infiltrates the renal parenchyma causing renal enlargement with preservation of the overall kidney shape.

stem: A 58-year-old man undergoes a cystoscopy for investigation of a urinary tract malignancy following presentation with haematuria. He is found to have a primary adenocarcinoma of the bladder.
prompt: Which of the following is the LEAST common site of this malignancy? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks for the LEAST likely answer.

Adenocarcinoma of the bladder

Certain areas within the bladder show an increased prevalence of adenocarcinoma - in particular, the bladder base, urethrocoeles (not technically bladder), and any urachal remnants found in the midline. Urachal remnant carcinomas account for around 30% of adenocarcinomas of the bladder. Carcinomas of the prostate are most commonly adenocarcinoma and although usually it is readily possible to differentiate between a prostatic malignancy and a bladder tumour on MRI, there may be advanced invasive cases where the line is more blurred. It is important clinically to differentiate between secondary adenocarcinomas which have metastasized from elsewhere and primary adenocarcinomas as the treatment is obviously very different. This is a histological diagnosis however, not radiological. Secondary adenocarcinomas are more common than primary adenocarcinomas.

For the most part, imaging is not able to distinguish between the different cell types with any degree of reliability; the diagnosis is histological.

Other bladder cancers:

| Cell type | Percentage |
| --- | --- |
| Transitional cell carcinoma | >90-95 |
| Squamous cell carcinoma | 2-15 (strong geographical variation) |
| Adenocarcinoma (primary) | <2 |
| Sarcoma | <2 |

Transitional cell carcinoma

Transitional carcinoma makes up around 95% of urinary tract cancers in the UK. The vast majority affect the bladder. The renal pelvis is the second most commonly affected site. The ureter is the least common site of malignancy. The lower third is affected in around 75% of cases, followed by the middle third. The proximal third is affected in only around 3% or ureteric malignancies. Bladder diverticulae, if present, pose an increased risk of tumour development due to urinary stasis within them. These also show invasive features at an earlier stage owing to the paucity of protective muscle surrounding them.

Smokers are at vastly increased risk of developing TCC due to the prolonged contact of carcinogens excreted in urine with the bladder wall.

Both SCC and adenocarcinomas of the bladder are linked to entities which cause chronic bladder irritation such as long term catheters, bladder stones and chronic urinary tract infection. In developing countries, infection with schistosomiasis strongly skews the prevalence data as it is known to cause squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

Urethral diverticulum (urethrocoele)

Dysuria, dyspareunia and post-void dribbling are classical for this condition. An outpouching of the urethral mucosa protrudes through the smooth muscle. This is seen on MRI as high T2 signal adjacent to or surrounding the urethra. Urinary stasis within the diverticulum predisposes patients to the formation of calculi, which can be seen as low signal on the T2 scan, and adenocarcinoma which will enhance with gadolinium.

Urachal cyst (extraprostatic)

The urachus is a fibrous remnant of a thin canal connecting the bladder to the umbilicus. Ordinarily it is almost imperceptible however there are four distinct anomalies which can persist into adulthood and cause symptoms.

Patency – a fistula between the bladder and the umbilicus. There is leakage of urine from the umbilicus present from birth.

Sinus – blind dilatation of the urachus at the umbilical end.

Diverticulum – communication with the dome of the bladder

Cyst – dilatation in the lower third which does not communicate with either end. These are asymptomatic unless or until the cyst becomes infected or ruptures.

MRI bladder

Imaging the bladder with MRI is a balancing act between sufficient distension to achieve adequate sensitivity rates without the images being compromised by motion due to the discomfort of having a full bladder for the duration of the scan.

On T2 the detrusor muscle returns low signal but the continuity of this layer will be disrupted if there is invasion.

The T1 images are more useful for evaluating lymph node involvement and any bony metastases.

Post-contrast images are of limited use in bladder cancer imaging. Some literature does support their use since the tumours tend to enhance early, whereas the muscle layer undergoes only delayed enhancement but since the bladder mucosa and submucosa also enhance in the early phase the appearances can be confusing to the untrained eye.

stem: A 64-year-old woman who is known to have had type 2 diabetes mellitus for many years is being investigated for recurrent urinary tract infections. A mid-stream urine specimen shows microscopic haematuria and she goes on to have a cystoscopy. At cystoscopy there are multiple bladder lesions measuring between 3-9mm in diameter which appear slightly raised from the mucosa and yellowish in colour. The findings are mirrored on an IVU which also shows filling defects in the distal right ureter.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Malakoplakia

Directly translated from Greek, malakoplakia just means soft plaques. These are actually submucosal inflammatory plaques consisting of basophilic PAS positive inclusion bodies and incompletely destroyed e-coli bacteria. The giveaway pathological term is Michaelis-Gutmann inclusion bodies which are the incompletely destroyed e-coli bacteria surrounded by a lipoprotein membrane. Although malakoplakia can occur in anyone, patients with diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression are predisposed to it. Importantly though, it is not a pre-malignant condition unlike leukoplakia. On imaging there are filling defects in the bladder and distal ureters. These are usually small, measuring only a few millimetres across.

Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP)

This curious condition results from chronic pyelonephritis and leads to a non-functioning kidney. Chronic infection (most commonly with Proteus or e-coli) induces a granulomatous process whereby the renal tissue eventually becomes replaced by a mass of reactive tissue. Since proteus infection is one of the main causes it is not surprising that many cases present with a staghorn calculus. The exact association varies from 30-90% depending on the data source. The other finding on CT is of multiple low attenuation rounded areas with Hounsfield Units (HU) of around -15 to -20. These are the dilated calyces filled with debris and xanthoma collections and they cause the whole kidney to be enlarged. The appearance is said to resemble a bear’s paw. Patients can present either on a background of recurrent UTIs or potentially renal colic. Vague malaise and weight loss may be the presentation in the absence of direct urinary symptoms.

Schistosomiasis

Schistosome larvae burrow through human skin and travel via the lymphatics to the lungs and liver to mature. Thence they continue onto the pelvic vessels where eggs are deposited in the bladder wall. There the eggs cause both a granulomatous and an inflammatory reaction which erodes through the bladder mucosa and the eggs are then excreted in the urine. The disease is endemic to many parts of Africa.

The dominant imaging feature is of bladder wall calcification. This is usually described as curvilinear or floccular and involves all of the layers of the bladder. Owing to the chronic fibrotic reaction the bladder eventually becomes restricted and small; thus the standout imaging feature is of a small calcified bladder. The main differential diagnosis of bladder wall calcification is tuberculosis.

Another important facet to these cases is the risk of bladder cancer developing in the context of chronic inflammation. These cancers are squamous cell carcinomas and should be actively looked for in cases of schistosomiasis; there is a latent period of approximately 20 years prior to development.

Renal tuberculosis

In areas of the world endemic to tuberculosis, renal tuberculosis is a reasonably common presentation of extra-pulmonary disease. The appearances on imaging vary depending on the disease timeline. The classical ‘putty kidney’ of renal tuberculosis is an end-stage appearance where there is dystrophic calcification affecting all parts of the kidney. At this point the kidney has usually become shrunken and small and the final appearance is of so-called autonephrectomy when there is essentially no parenchymal tissue left, just amorphous calcification. An earlier manifestation is stenosis to the infundibuli connecting the calyces to the renal pelvis causing proximal dilatation of the calyces which are seen to be clubbed on a urogram. Purportedly, the earliest sign is of moth-eaten calyces owing to uneven erosion to the papillae.

Leukoplakia

Directly translated from Greek, leukoplakia just means white plaques. It is a squamous metaplastic condition affecting the transitional cell epithelium of the bladder. Presentation is usually as a consequence either of recurrent urinary tract infections or urinary tract calculi. Sometimes patients complain of passing flaky white tissue in the urine which is pathognomonic for this condition. On imaging there is mucosal thickening and filling defects within the bladder. Some sources consider leukoplakia to be a premalignant condition for epidermoid carcinoma.

stem: A 40-year-old lady undergoes a colposcopy for an abnormal smear result. The registrar notices some small yellowish lumps on the surface of the cervix.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Anatomy is the key to differentiating between the various female urogenital cysts most of which are, for the most part, asymptomatic incidental findings.

Skene duct cyst

These are retention cysts of the paraurethral ducts and usually they are asymptomatic. On MRI they are seen inferior to the pubic symphysis but lateral to the external urethral meatus. Signal characteristics reflect their cystic nature with high T2 signal but fluid-fluid levels may also be present if there has been intracystic haemorrhage.

Bartholin gland cyst

The bartholin glands secrete lubricating fluid into the inferior third of the vagina. They are found in highest numbers at the posterolateral aspect of the inferior vagina. Although usually asymptomatic, when infected or inflamed a Bartholin gland cyst can present as a painful lump. On MRI they show as high T1 signal owing to the mucoid fluid.

Urethral diverticulum (also known as urethrocele)

Dysuria, dyspareunia and post-void dribbling are classical for this condition. An outpouching of the urethral mucosa protrudes through the smooth muscle. This is seen on MRI as high T2 signal adjacent to or surrounding the urethra. Urinary stasis within the diverticulum predisposes patients to the formation of calculi, which can be seen as low signal on the T2 scan, and adenocarcinoma which will enhance with gadolinium.

Nabothian cyst

Blockage of the mucinous glands on the cervix causes tiny fluid-filled structures to form. These are asymptomatic and appear as small yellow bumps on colposcopy. On MRI they are cystic with high T2 signal and can show high T1 signal owing to their mucein content. They are an incidental finding.

Gartner duct cyst

These are usually found incidentally on MRI scans but can cause dyspareunia. They do not communicate with the urethra and would be unlikely to cause post-void dribbling. They are remnants of the Wolffian ducts and occur superiorly in the anterolateral wall of the vagina. On imaging they appear straightforwardly cystic. For the most part they occur sporadically but they can also be seen in conjunction with renal agenesis or ectopia and are also typical of a rare condition called Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich syndrome. This condition causes duplication of all or part of the female genital tract with unilateral haematometrocolpos and ipsilateral renal agenesis.

Ectopic ureter

The ureter normally inserts into the trigone of the bladder but ectopic insertions do occur. If these are below the external urethral sphincter the patient may experience dribbling symptoms however these are likely to have been present from birth. An ectopic ureter may be an isolated diagnosis or may form part of a VACTERL presentation and there is an affiliation to renal duplexity. Vesico-ureteric reflux is also very common since the normal valve mechanism is not present to prevent it. Abnormal ureteric anatomy is well demonstrated either with fluoroscopic studies or a highly T2 weighted sequence on an MRI scan.

stem: A 63-year-old lady develops progressive abdominal distension accompanied by vague abdominal pains. An ultrasound shows a 20cm complex ovarian mass and her ca-125 level is found to be markedly elevated. She undergoes a CT scan for staging and widespread disease is discovered.
prompt: Which of the following is least likely to be secondary to metastatic ovarian cancer?
explanation:
Bony involvement in metastatic ovarian cancer is actually relatively uncommon with only around 2% of patients being affected.

Ovarian cancer can spread in a multitude of ways:

| Spread of ovarian cancer |  |
| --- | --- |
| Direct extension | Sigmoid mesocolon, broad ligament, fallopian tubes |
| Intraperitoneal seeding and implantation | Omental caking, peritoneal space |
| Lymphatic spread | External iliac, obturator nodes |
| Haematogenous | Liver, lung, adrenal glands, pleural effusion |

Bowel obstruction is relatively common cause of morbidity and mortality with disseminated ovarian cancer.

Ovarian cancer

There are a number of different types of ovarian carcinoma and the final diagnosis will be a histological one. On imaging the features can be varied.

| Subtypes | Frequency and age |
| --- | --- |
| Malignant epithelial tumours (Serous, mucinous, endometroid, clear cell) | 85% 60s -70s |
| Malignant germ cell tumours (Teratoma, dysgerminaoma, choricarcinoma, mixed) | 7% <30 years |
| Metastases | <10% |
| Sex cord stromal tumours | ~5% |

A number of factors increase the risk of developing ovarian cancer in an individual. Anything which increases the number of ovulatory cycles a woman undergoes in her lifetime will increase the risk of ovarian cancer (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity), and vice versa (multiparity, breastfeeding, oral contraceptive pill use). A family history of related cancers also increase the risk.

Presenting symptoms may be quite vague with abdominal pains, constipation or urinary frequency being the only complaints if any from the patient. Consequently many tumours have already spread beyond the ovary by the time of diagnosis. Initial investigation is often with ultrasound. Although ovarian cancers can have a variety of imaging appearances, solid or papillary components to a cystic mass are strongly indicative of malignancy. Predominantly solid masses with some small cystic components are also likely to be malignant but completely perfectly solid lesions are actually more likely to be benign. Ovarian fibromas and fibrothecomas are both benign lesions which can be seen as solid masses however despite this, without prior imaging for comparison a solid ovarian lesion is malignant until proven otherwise.

Ovarian cysts

The incidental finding of a simple (non-haemorrhagic) ovarian cyst in day to day cross-sectional reporting is a relatively common occurrence. In deciding on a subsequent management plan both age and the size of the cyst should be taken into account as well as the presence of any internal haemorrhage, thus:

| Age | Diameter | Plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reproductive age | <3cm | Normal finding, no follow up |
|  | 3-5cm | Almost certainly benign, no follow up |
|  | 5-7cm | Almost certainly benign but risk of torsion. Follow up with ultrasound either at 2-6 months if uncertainty of findings, or at 6-12 months. |
|  | >7cm | Difficult to fully evaluate on ultrasound, suggest MRI |
|  | Haemorrhagic, >5cm | Follow up ultrasound or MRI in 6 weeks (different part of the menstrual cycle) |
| Post-menopausal | <1cm | No follow up |
|  | 1-3 cm | Describe but no follow up needed. |
|  | 3-5 cm | Follow up with ultrasound either at 3-6 months if uncertainty of findings, or at 6-12 months. |
|  | Haemorrhagic, any size | Follow up ultrasound or MRI in 6 weeks |

In summary if a cyst is above 7cm in diameter an MRI is warranted even though the likelihood of benignity is still extremely high.
