explanation:
Gynaecomastia

Gynaecomastia is typically described as a ‘flame-shaped’ mass. It is usually bilateral but unilateral in a third of cases with two thirds of those cases involving the left breast only. There are a number of drugs which are associated with the development of gynaecomastia including spironolactone, a diuretic used in the treatment of heart failure. Other medications include isoniazid (anti-TB drug), tricyclic antidepressants, steroids, and oestrogens. Marijuana use has also been linked to gynaecomastia. Patients suffering from diseases with hormone production or hormone imbalances can also develop gynaecomastia. These include alcoholism, Klinefelter syndrome, hepatoblastoma, fibrolamellar carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, and testicular tumours. There is no correlation between gynaecomastia and male breast cancer.

stem: A 72-year-old man is undergoing pre-operative assessment prior to a routine TURP procedure for some troublesome lower urinary tract symptoms. When his PSA is found to be markedly elevated he undergoes an MRI scan for further investigation.
prompt: Which of the following regarding prostate cancer in the transitional zone is correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: They often have extraprostatic disease at presentation
A negative trans-rectal biopsy is reassuring
A non-circumscribed low T2 lesion is most likely to be BPH
Around 30% of prostate cancers occur in the transitional zone
They can be easily distinguished from BPH changes
explanation:
Transitional zone cancers are less common than peripheral zone cancers but do occur and account for around 30% of prostate cancers. They are often harder to detect clinically due to their central location, and can be occult on imaging owing to overlap and confusion, in particular in patients with benign prostatic hypertrophy since it is the transitional zone which is involved in BPH. BPH leads to a heterogenous and enlarged appearance to the transitional zone which can obscure smaller lesions. On the plus side however, they are more often organ-confined since their central location effectively cushions them from capsular breach for longer. Their central location within the prostate cancer does however mean that trans-rectal biopsies may be falsely reassuring if negative, having missed the lesion due to lesion-depth within the prostate. Clinicians should have a low threshold for repeat-biopsies.

Peripheral zone

The highest grade of suspicion for malignancy in the peripheral zone is indicated by the presence of marked restricted diffusion (focal high b-value and corresponding low ADC signal), with a PIRADS 5 lesion being one that is greater than 1.5 cm. PIRADS 3 lesions will show some restricted diffusion but this is far less (subjective analysis) than for PIRADS 4 lesions. Dynamic contrast enhancement is used for assessment of peripheral zone lesions only - differentiating between lesions which show only limited restricted diffusion. If there is dynamic contrast enhancement with a type 3 washout curve, the lesion becomes a PIRADS 4 lesion despite the only limited restriction in diffusion.

Transitional zone

The highest grade of suspicion for transitional zone lesions is reserved for moderate T2 lesion which is lenticular or non-circumscribed and moderately T2 hypointense (PIRADS 5 >1.5 cm).

Three plane T2 imaging is common practice and enables full assessment of the peripheral zone of the prostate, particularly examining for extra-capsular extension, bladder base or seminal vesical invasion. T2 is also the most important sequence for lesions in the transitional zone.

The T1 weighted sequences are also useful to check for the presence of any haemorrhagic foci although since most patients now undergo their MRI scan prior to any biopsies being taken this has become far less important.

Interestingly the ADC map is more sensitive for carcinoma of the prostate (in the peripheral zone) than the DWI sequences. A finding of focal low signal on the ADC map may be seen in the absence of a corresponding high DWI focus. In the transitional zone however, the T2 sequences are more sensitive.

stem: A 72-year-old man is undergoing pre-operative assessment prior to a routine TURP procedure for some troublesome lower urinary tract symptoms. When his PSA is found to be slightly elevated he undergoes an MRI scan for further investigation. A 12mm nodule is seen in the left peripheral zone. It returns high signal on the T2 weighted sequence. Dynamic contrast enhancement analysis reveals a curve with a gently increasing intensity.
prompt: What type of curve is being described? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Axial dynamic contrast enhanced imaging (after non-contrast axial T1) is essential to differentiate between between PIRADS 3 and 4 lesions. The three types of curve are known as type 1-2 curves. Type 3 curves are considered most suspicious for prostate cancer. Just like for breast cancer contrast enhancement curves, in a metabolically active lesion there is usually rapid uptake and rapid washout of contrast, leading to the classical type 3 curve. Type 1 and 2 curves in prostate imaging can also occur in malignant lesions but type 3 curves are the most concerning.

stem: A 72 -year-old lady develops new post menopausal bleeding and is referred by her GP for an ultrasound. This shows a thickened endometrium of 15mm with underlying cystic areas.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select one answer only.
explanation:
It is usually not possible to definitely separate Tamoxifen related change from Endometrial cancer on imaging appearances alone and a biopsy would be required however although the patient in the vignette absolutely should be sent for a biopsy, the question is asking which is the most likely diagnosis (as opposed to which is the diagnosis which should be excluded before considering tamoxifen related changes). Metastatic breast cancer must also be considered in the differential diagnosis and adenomyosis can also appear as cystic areas within an apparently thickened endometrium.

Tamoxifen

Tamoxifen works against the usual effects of oestrogen by binding to oestrogen receptors however where the background level of oestrogen is very low it can have oestrogenic effects on the uterine endometrium. Endometrial polyps, subendometrial cysts and an increase in the thickness have all been associated with tamoxifen therapy. For this reason patients experiencing abnormal bleeding whilst taking tamoxifen should be investigated with hysteroscopy as first line management, instead of ultrasound.

HRT

Hormone replacement therapy in post-menopausal women can also cause an increase in the endometrial thickness. It should not be taken as a sign of benignity however, and tissue sampling must still be sought. The presence of subendometrial cysts would be unusual.

Adenomyosis

Adenomyosis and endometrial cancer can be hard to distinguish in some patients and both can show increased vascularity. Adenomyosis affects the myometrium whereas endometrial cancer arises from the endometrium. Thought by some to be a variant on the theme of endometriosis, adenomyosis is the ectopic presence of endometrial tissue within the myometrium. Its presence also causes smooth muscle proliferation. Adenomyosis can occur either diffusely or be limited to a focal area. On an HSG there will be small diverticuli but on MRI the classical description is of widening of the transitional zone (aka junctional zone; the inner layer of myometrium) to greater than 12mm. Small areas of high T1 and T2 signal are seen representing areas of haemorrhage and cystic change respectively.

Factors linked to an increased risk of endometrial cancer:

Iatrogenic oestrogens

Tamoxifen

Early menarch or late menopause

No children

PCOS

Obesity

Diabetes

Endometrial cancer

Anything that increases unopposed oestrogen exposure causes an increased risk of endometrial cancer. For the most part it is a disease of the post-menopausal age group and thus presents with post-menopausal bleeding but around 10% of cases present prior to this with irregular bleeding. Initial investigation is often with ultrasound where any endometrial thickness of >5mm in a postmenopausal lady would be suspicious. < 5mm of endometrial thickness has a 100% negative predictive value for endometrial carcinoma. Where there is a poorly defined interface between the endometrium and the myometrium, invasive carcinoma should be considered. Cellular diagnosis can be obtained at hysteroscopy, with dilatation and curettage or a pipelle biopsy.

| Phase | Days in cycle/th> | Endometrial thickness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Menstrual | 1-7 | 1-4mm |
| Proliferative | 7-14 | 5-7mm |
| Periovulatory | 14 | 11mm |
| Secretory | 14-28 | 16mm |
| Post-menopausal | - | <5mm |

MRI is used for staging where it is the T2 weighted sequences which provide the most information. The myometrium and endometrium are separated by a black stripe called the junctional zone (aka transitional zone; the inner layer of myometrium). The endometrial cancer causes loss of the bright endometrial signal and breach of this black junctional zone denotes myometrial invasion. On T1 weighted images the layers are all isointense to one another. A crucial staging change comes with cervical invasion which denotes stage II. Fertility sparing management (if required) is no longer a viable option and lymph node sampling is usually done at hysterectomy to detect any involved nodes which, if present, would upstage the patient to stage III. Endometrial cancer spread via the lymph nodes can involve any of the pelvic lymph node groups (with the exception of inguinal nodes which are non-regional for endometrial cancer), and the para-aortic lymph nodes. Indeed the para-aortic lymph nodes can sometimes be enlarged in the absence of pelvic lymph node involvement so careful examination of all the lymph node groups must be performed.

Contrast is required for endometrial cancer staging in order to accurately assess the depth of myometrial invasion. Blood and blood degradation products are common features of uterine imaging and separating these from tumour is important. The tumours tend to enhance early, earlier than the endometrium, but to a lesser degree than the strongly enhancing myometrium. Images are usually taken at around 3-4 minutes post-contrast. Contrast images also help evaluate for invasion of the cervical stroma, a feature which carries the patient up to stage II if present. Contrast is also used in the staging of ovarian tumours but rectal tumours and cervical cancer are the pelvic tumours which do not use contrast for staging. The literature is divided as to whether it is useful for staging bladder cancers.

stem: You are performing an ultrasound scan on a 65-year-old lady who was referred by her GP after finding a lump in her left breast. At the site of the lump, you can see a well-defined oval shaped soft tissue breast lesion.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Phyllodes tumour

These would typically be described as having a similar appearance to a fibroadenoma. They would usually appear as a lobulated round hypoechoic mass with ill-defined borders and a posterior acoustic enhancement. Occasionally they can demonstrate a ‘halo’ sign. Patients are usually middle aged, slightly older than those with a fibroadenoma.

Fibroadenoma

Popcorn calcification is pathognomonic of a fibroadenoma. They tend to be nodular or lobulated in contour but with smooth margins. They often show a ‘halo’ sign of low attenuation where tissue surrounding the lesion has been compressed. Patients are usually relatively young; 20s or 30s.

Galactocoele

A galactocoele appears during lactation as an enlarging painless mass. A fat-fluid level is a specific finding on a lateral view. These lesions would be far more likely to be ultrasound diagnoses than mammographic. They can have a variety of appearances, ranging from cystic with internal debris, to solid appearing masses. Posterior acoustic is an important feature which suggests a fluid component to the mass. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by aspirating milk from the lesion.

Breast abscess

Clinical manifestations notwithstanding, would appear cystic on ultrasound.

Radial scar

The classic description of a radial scar used to be in a patient with prior breast surgery. Actually, there is no association with prior surgery. Around half are associated with a carcinoma and hence management is usually surgical excision.

stem: A 65-year-old man is found to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm when he undergoes an ultrasound scan as part of the national screening service. He is followed up with a CT scan which also shows that he has no kidney on his right side. His left kidney measures 18cm in length. Review of the ultrasound images shows no interpolar notch.
prompt: What is the diagnosis?
options: Right renal agenesis and left renal hypertrophy
explanation:
Renal agenesis

Agenesis is associated with many chromosomal aberrations including the trisomies and Turner syndrome. Additionally it is seen in conjunction with Mullerian duct anomalies, VACTERL anomalies and many others. Bilateral renal agenesis results in Potter sequence (oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia) and is currently incompatible with life. Unilateral renal agenesis results in compensatory hypertrophy of the remaining kidney and care must be taken therefore, not to mistake the condition for crossed fused renal ectopia which some sources say is more common.

Crossed fused renal ectopia

Crossed renal ectopia occurs when both kidneys ascend on one side during embryological development. In crossed fused renal ectopia they are fused as well. Like horseshoe kidney it is a malformation which is twice as commonly seen in men as in women. The condition can be complicated by infections and stones. An ultrasound will show an apparently enlarged single kidney although careful examination reveals a notch between two distinct kidneys which have fused. Angiography is necessary prior to any surgical intervention owing to the propensity for vascular aberrancy of morphologically abnormal kidneys.

Horseshoe kidney

When the kidneys are fused at the poles they fail to ascend properly during development, meeting resistance at the inferior mesenteric artery. In 90% of cases it is the lower poles which have fused leading to the classical horseshoe appearance. The ureters course anteriorly over the fused portion and are prone to reflux. The anterior displacement of the fused kidneys renders them susceptible to damage from abdominal trauma whereas, by comparison, kidneys in their usual location are protected by the lower ribs. Horseshoe kidneys are twice as commonly seen in men as in women and have numerous associations, chiefly genitourinary in nature but also, notably, trisomy. The giveaway description on imaging is of medially orientated renal long axes in addition to the anterior course followed by both ureters. Horseshoe kidney may be an incidental diagnosis but since patients are at greater risk of developing urinary tract infections, calculi, and transitional cell carcinoma, presentation may relate to one of these.

Prune Belly Syndrome also known as Eagle-Barrett syndrome

This is a triad of:

Abdominal wall muscle deficiency

Distension of the distal ureters +/- hydronephrosis

Bilateral cryptorchidism

Despite the final element to the triad the condition can occur in girls but is far less common. There is a multitude of associations spanning all the other body systems which can occur in conjunction with this disease. Around one third of babies die within the first 24 months but where renal function is less affected the prognosis is much better.

Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome also known as EMG syndrome (Exomphalos, Macroglossia, Gigantism)

This curious condition crops up in a number of different radiology circles. It is caused by a mutation on chromosome 11 and leads to a specific set of clinical manifestations, chief among them are the three which give it the alternative name of EMG syndrome. Malrotation of the small intestine is another feature which has a high concordance with this condition.

stem: A 72-year-old man is undergoing pre-operative assessment prior to a routine TURP procedure for some troublesome lower urinary tract symptoms. When his PSA is found to be slightly elevated he undergoes an MRI scan for further investigation. A 12mm tumour is seen in the left peripheral zone. It returns low signal on the T2 weighted sequences. Dynamic contrast enhancement analysis reveals a curve with an initial upslope followed by a plateau phase.
prompt: What type of curve is being described? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Axial dynamic contrast enhanced imaging (after non-contrast axial T1) is essential to differentiate between between PIRADS 3 and 4 lesions. The three types of curve are known as type 1-2 curves. Type 3 curves are considered most suspicious for prostate cancer. Just like for breast cancer contrast enhancement curves, in a metabolically active lesion there is usually rapid uptake and rapid washout of contrast, leading to the classical type 3 curve. Type 1 and 2 curves in prostate imaging can also occur in malignant lesions but type 3 curves are the most concerning.

PIRADS curves © Medical Exam Prep

The assessment of peripheral zone and central zone lesions is very different in PIRADS assessment.

Peripheral zone

The highest grade of suspicion for malignancy in the peripheral zone is indicated by the presence of marked restricted diffusion (focal high b-value and corresponding low ADC signal), with a PIRADS 5 lesion being one that is greater than 1.5 cm. PIRADS 3 lesions will show some restricted diffusion but this is far less (subjective analysis) than for PIRADS 4 lesions. Dynamic contrast enhancement is used for assessment of peripheral zone lesions only - differentiating between lesions which show only limited restricted diffusion. If there is dynamic contrast enhancement with a type 3 washout curve, the lesion becomes a PIRADS 4 lesion despite the only limited restriction in diffusion.

Transitional zone

The highest grade of suspicion for transitional zone lesions is reserved for moderate T2 lesion which is lenticular or non-circumscribed and moderately T2 hypointense (PIRADS 5 >1.5 cm).

Three plane T2 imaging is common practice and enables full assessment of the peripheral zone of the prostate, particularly examining for extra-capsular extension, bladder base or seminal vesical invasion. T2 is also the most important sequence for lesions in the transitional zone.

Diffusion weighted imaging is essential for PIRADS calculation and is the first sequence that should be used to evaluate lesions in the peripheral zone.

The T1 weighted sequences are also useful to check for the presence of any haemorrhagic foci although since most patients now undergo their MRI scan prior to any biopsies being taken this has become far less important.

Interestingly the ADC map is more sensitive for carcinoma of the prostate (in the peripheral zone) than the DWI sequences. A finding of focal low signal on the ADC map may be seen in the absence of a corresponding high DWI focus. In the transitional zone however, the T2 sequences are more sensitive.

stem: A 35-year-old lady is involved in an RTA. She is stabilised at the scene and evacuated via helicopter to the trauma centre where she undergoes an immediate trauma CT. This shows, among lesser injuries, that the left kidney has sustained significant trauma.
prompt: Which of the following on CT would indicate the LEAST severe renal injury?
options: Laceration involving the left renal pelvis
Subcapsular haematoma of the left kidney
explanation:
The priorities as far as surgery are concerned are:

Haemostasis

Preserving renal viability

Any injury which threatens either of these is an indication for urgent intervention. A vascular pedicle injury provides a significant threat to the viability of the kidney.

Traumatic injuries to the kidneys are graded according to the depth of parenchymal damage and the presence or absence of active bleeding.

| Grade V | Renal artery or vein distruption with active bleedingNear/complete infarction with active bleeding>3 segments injured with active bleeding |
| Bilateral injuries | Each kidney is graded separately |

stem: A 43-year-old woman undergoes a renal ultrasound scan for recurrent urinary tract infections. This demonstrates hyperechoic renal pyramids with posterior acoustic shadowing suggestive of cortical nephrocalcinosis.
prompt: Which of the following is a recognised cause of cortical nephrocalcinosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Disseminated pneumocystis causes cortical necrosis and calcification, similar to disseminated MAI. The other conditions are associated with medullary nephrocalcinosis. Incidentally, medullary nephrocalcinosis is 20 times more common than cortical nephrocalcinosis.

The most common cause of nephrocalcinosis is hyperparathyroidism (followed closely by renal tubular acidosis). Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Beckwith-Weidman (as well as Caroli disease) are associated with medullary sponge kidney (which should always be considered if there is unilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis.

| Hyperparathyroidism | Acute cortical necrosis |
| Renal tubular acidosis (most common cause in children) | Chronic transplant rejection |
| Medullary sponge kidney | Alport syndrome |
| Renal papillary necrosis (ischaemia) |  |
| Sarcoidosis |  |

stem: You are reviewing the images of a 72-year-old man. He has had an MRI scan following an incidental finding of an elevated PSA during pre-op screening for an elective TURP. The scan shows an enlarged prostate gland with diffusely low T2 signal affecting the whole gland. Prostate biopsies show no malignancy and you suspect that the MRI appearance is caused by granulomatous prostatitis.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a possible aetiology for this condition? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT a possible aetiology for this condition.

This patient has granulomatous prostatitis. This is an unusual condition which is said to develop following intravesical BCG therapy for bladder cancer. Other possible causes are sarcoidosis or tuberculous prostatitis. Aside from these, more recently purely idiopathic cases have also been noted. In these cases a recent UTI or urethral instrumentation have been implicated. The imaging appearances are reminiscent of a PI-RADS 5/5 prostate cancer and the diagnosis should always be made histologically. Whatever the aetiology, the patient followed up to resolution of imaging abnormalities to ensure a prostate cancer has not been masked.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the prostate accounts for very few prostate cancers. The majority are adenocarcinoma or transitional cell carcinoma.

stem: You are performing an ultrasound scan on a 27-year-old lady. She has presented with severe abdominal pain and is on day 7 of her menstrual cycle. You suspect she may have ovarian torsion.
prompt: Which of the following regarding this diagnosis is NOT correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: Small fluid pockets seen around the edge of the ovary are in-keeping with the diagnosis
The diagnosis is not excluded by the presence of doppler flow in the ovary
The most common cause of ovarian torsion is a tubo-ovarian abscess
The ovary will be larger than normal
Torsion is more common during early pregnancy
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT correct.

Ovarian torsion

At least half of all ovarian torsion is caused by a lead point (i.e. an ovarian mass). Most cases are due to a corpus luteum cyst or follicular cyst with a dermoid cyst being the next most common cause. Torsion is also more common during early pregnancy than in non-pregnant patients. On ultrasound the ovary itself will be enlarged (>4cm in length), and heterogenously echogenic. In the periphery of the ovary, small fluid-filled follicles may be appreciated. On doppler ultrasound scan, twisting of the ovarian pedicle is a useful sign but actual flow within the ovary itself does not exclude torsion since it is venous flow which is lost first.

Symptoms may resolve spontaneously with de-torsion but otherwise laparoscopy is indicated to de-tort the ovary and remove any lead point. If the ovary is infarcted at the time of surgery this will also be resected.

Mature teratoma

(Immature) teratomas and dermoid cysts (mature teratomas) have very similar imaging characteristics despite their histological differences. Teratomas are the most common ovarian neoplasm but are slow growing and usually benign. By contrast immature teratomas are malignant. The presence of fat is a strong indicator for a mature teratoma with the combination of fat, fluid and calcification being highly specific. On MRI the fat will show the usual signal drop-out on fat saturated sequences. Calcification will show as low signal on T2. Although benign, mature teratomas can be complicated by torsion or rupture. Malignant degeneration if it does occur, is to squamous cell carcinoma most commonly.

Mature teratomas can have a variety of appearances on ultrasound scan depending on their internal composition. Posterior acoustic shadowing suggests the presence of calcification.

The corpus luteum

The corpus luteum consists of the remnant of a ruptured ovarian follicle following ovulation. It produces oestrogen and progesterone to sustain a pregnancy following fertilisation. On ultrasound it is seen as a thick-walled cyst with peripheral vascularity on colour Doppler flow. This 'ring of fire' appearance can be confused with an ectopic pregnancy.

Ovarian torsion

At least half of all ovarian torsion is caused by a lead point (i.e. an ovarian mass). Most cases are due to a corpus luteum cyst or follicular cyst with a dermoid cyst being the next most common cause. Torsion is also more common during early pregnancy than in non-pregnant patients. On ultrasound the ovary itself will be enlarged (>4cm in length), and heterogenously echogenic. In the periphery of the ovary, small fluid-filled follicles may be appreciated. On doppler ultrasound scan, twisting of the ovarian pedicle is a useful sign but actual flow within the ovary itself does not exclude torsion since it is venous flow which is lost first.

Symptoms may resolve spontaneously with de-torsion but otherwise laparoscopy is indicated to de-tort the ovary and remove any lead point. If the ovary is infarcted at the time of surgery this will also be resected.
Mature teratoma

(Immature) teratomas and dermoid cysts (mature teratomas) have very similar imaging characteristics despite their histological differences. Teratomas are the most common ovarian neoplasm but are slow growing and usually benign. By contrast immature teratomas are malignant. The presence of fat is a strong indicator for a mature teratoma with the combination of fat, fluid and calcification being highly specific. On MRI the fat will show the usual signal drop-out on fat saturated sequences. Calcification will show as low signal on T2. Although benign, mature teratomas can be complicated by torsion or rupture. Malignant degeneration if it does occur, is to squamous cell carcinoma most commonly.
Mature teratomas can have a variety of appearances on ultrasound scan depending on their internal composition. Posterior acoustic shadowing suggests the presence of calcification.
The corpus luteum

The corpus luteum consists of the remnant of a ruptured ovarian follicle following ovulation. It produces oestrogen and progesterone to sustain a pregnancy following fertilisation. On ultrasound it is seen as a thick-walled cyst with peripheral vascularity on colour Doppler flow. This 'ring of fire' appearance can be confused with an ectopic pregnancy.

stem: You are reporting a CT abdomen of a 45-year-old man who has presented to A+E with loin to groin pain and haematuria. As well as a small ureteric calculus, you notice a cyst in the upper pole of the left kidney which has four apparently enhancing thin septae within it. There is no calcification.
prompt: What should your recommendation be?
options: Follow up at 6 months, then yearly for 5 years
explanation:
**Based on Bosniak Classification 2019**

Bosniak classification

The Bosniak classification of renal cysts is based on their CT or MRI features and provides a guide to follow up based on the likelihood of malignancy. The cyst described is a Bosniak IIF. The following table simplifies the classification.

A lesion with <25% enhancing tissue. If more than a quarter of a lesion is enhancing then this is potentially a necrosing solid tumour instead.

Terms complicated/complex cysts should be avoided

Bosniak I and II lesions can be termed cysts

Bosniak IIF, III and IV can be termed cystic renal masses.

Should not be used for syndromes (von Hippel Lindau, hereditary leiomyomatosis, RCC syndromes) due to high rate of RCCs in lesions which appear cystic, even down to Bosniak I.

| Bosniak Classification | Malignancy | Findings | Follow up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | ~0% | </= 2mm smooth wall (can enhance)Simple fluid -9 to 20 HU | None |
| II | ~0% | </= 2 mm smooth wall1-3 septa>/= 70 HU on non-contrast CT>20 HU on any CT-9 to 20 HU on non-contrast CT21-30HU on portal venous CT (i.e. less than 10 HU of enhancement post contrast).Too small to characterise | None |
| IIF | 5% | 3 mm smooth wall or septal thickening>/= 4 smooth septa of >/= 2 mm thickness | 6 months.Then yearly for 5 years |
| III | 50% | Walls or septa are >/= 4 mm thick or irregularly enhancing. | Surgical resection or RFA via MDT |
| IV | >90% | >/= 1 enhancing nodule or protrusion (>/= 4 mm wide) | Surgical resection via MDT |

stem: A 30-year-old man is reviewed in the breast clinic following the development of gynaecomastia. He is on no medications which might provoke this and denies the use of any performance-enhancing steroids. A testicular ultrasound is performed which shows a mass in the left testicle.
prompt: Which of the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
For a patient to develop gynaecomastia as a consequence of testicular cancer the tumour must be oestrogenic. Sex cord stromal tumours can produce oestrogen and present in this way, as can germ cell tumours. The classical tumour to be linked with gynaecomastia as an index presentation is the sex cord tumour Leydig cell tumours since around a third of cases present as gynaecomastia. That being said, when tumour incidence is accounted for, technically more patients who present with gynaecomastia will actually have a germ cell tumour of either a seminomatous or non-seminomatous variety. If germ cell tumours are therefore pitched against sex cord tumours in a question the exact wording of the question is crucial. Certainly Leydig cell tumours (Sex cord tumours) are more closely linked with gynaecomastia but there are undeniably fewer of them.

| Tumour | % presentation with gynaecomastia | % of all testicular tumours | % of all testicular tumours presenting with gynaecomastia |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sex cord - Leydig cell | 30 | 1-3 | <9 |
| Sex cord - Sertoli cell | 3 | <1 | <1 |
| Germ cell - Seminoma | 5 | 25 | 12.5 |
| Germ cell - Non-seminomatous | 5 | 25 | 12.5 |

Sex cord stromal tumours

These account in total for only around 10% of testicular tumours but have some interesting characteristics.

Leydig cell tumours - classically these cause hormone imbalance and can present as gynaecomastia. Around a third of patients will present in this way. Most of these tumours are actually benign. There are two peaks in age prevalance at 5-10years and 20-30years

Sertoli cell tumours - These are much less common, less likely to produce hormones and therefore gynaecomastia but can be associated with syndromes such as Peutz-Jegher syndrome, or the Carney syndrome. They classically arise in young boys but are by no means rare at all any age.

| Carney Triad | Carney syndrome |
| --- | --- |
| Pulmonary hamartoma | Atrial myxoma |
| Gastric leiomyosarcoma (GIST) | Facial/buccal pigmentation |
| Extra-adrenal paraganglioma | Sertoli tumour of the testis |
|  | Pituitary adenoma |

Germ cell tumours

Germ cell tumours are divided into seminomas and non-seminomatous varieties. They are very common and comprise almost half of all testicular tumours. They can often be found incidentally or subsequent to any trauma which might cause the patient to self-examine and discover a testicular lump. Alternatively they can present as a vague dull scrotal aching sensation with no lump.

Lymphatic drainage is to the retroperitoneum. Para-aortic lymph nodes are therefore regional. Involvement of the internal, external and common iliac nodes however, is considered non-regional. Only if there has been previous scrotal or inguinal surgery disrupting tissue planes are inguinal or external iliac artery nodes considered regional.

They typically are found in patients in their 40s. Testicular tumours can be diagnosed with a strong pre-test probability based solely on age as detailed in the table below. On ultrasound there will be an intratesticular low reflectivity well-defined mass. Colour doppler flow can be seen within the mass.

| Age at diagnosis | Tumour |
| --- | --- |
| 10s | Yolk sac tumour or teratoma |
| 20s + 30s | Choriocarcinoma |
| 30s | Embryonal cell carcinoma |
| 40s | Seminoma |
